page_hint: Ch 4, Table 4-1 (Economic constraints row); Ch 4 §3 'Economic Constraints' bullets; Ch 4 §3 sidebar table 'what the ~$15,000 budget line is, and the 6–21-host workload comparison'; Ch 4 §8 mini-case closing paragraph
quoted_clause: at the ~6-host average the whole-fleet spend is ~$120/hour, giving **~2.76M input and ~90K output tokens per cloud dollar** ... Meeting the canonical ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak needs ~6–21 hosts, so the workload's real monthly spend is ~$87.6K–$306.6K/mo ... Cloud, 21 hosts always-on at peak | $306,600 | ≈ $49.13
observed: The canonical economic headline (Table 4-1 Economic row, the §3 'Throughput per dollar' and 'Cost per request' bullets, the sidebar table, and the §8 mini-case) is priced on a 6-host average / 21-host peak fleet. Those are the *full-utilization* KV-screen counts (⌈86/17⌉ = 6; ⌈344/17⌉ = 21). The same chapter's own mini-case states the book's provisioning policy produces ~31 hosts at the 70% × 95% screen (32 with the N−1 spare) at the canonical 40 rps peak — and the same policy applied to the average gives ⌈86/(17×0.70×0.95)⌉ = 8, +1 N−1 = 9 hosts. The cost table therefore prices a fleet the book itself says is not the fleet it would deploy, and the mini-case's own parenthetical ('the canonical 40 rps peak ... sizes to ~21 hosts full-util / ~31 working at the 70% × 95% policy (32 with N−1)') sits in direct contradiction of the cost table two paragraphs earlier.
evidence: Recomputation from the book's own inputs: full-util counts 6 (avg) and 21 (peak); policy counts 9 (avg) and 32 (peak). Peak always-on monthly spend: 32 × $20/hr × 730 hr = $467,200 vs the printed $306,600 (a 52% understatement). Average fleet spend: 9 × $20 = $180/hr vs the printed $120/hr. Headline tokens-per-dollar: 92,000 ÷ ($180/3600) = 1.84M input tokens per dollar vs the printed ~2.76M (a 50% overstatement); at peak, 368,000 ÷ ($640/3600) = 2.07M vs 3.15M on the 21-host basis. Owned per-request cost: (9×$20)/(10×3600) = ~$0.0050 and (32×$20)/(40×3600) = ~$0.0044, vs the printed ~$0.0033 / ~$0.0029.
root_cause: Two different fleet-sizing bases (full-utilization KV screen vs the 70% × 95% + N−1 provisioning policy) coexist in one chapter, and the economic layer silently adopts the former while the sizing layer states the latter. The book has no single named 'canonical fleet size' constant, so each consumer picks a different one.
correction: Pick one basis and state it once in the Canonical Workload box (recommended: the policy fleet, 9 hosts average / 32 hosts peak, with the full-util 6/21 shown as the un-headroomed lower bound). Then recompute: whole-fleet $/hr, tokens-per-dollar, owned $/request, and the sidebar's monthly and per-1K-req figures from that basis. If the 6/21 basis is retained for continuity with Ch 16–17, label every derived economic figure 'full-utilization, no headroom' and add a parallel policy-basis column rather than presenting the full-util numbers as 'the workload's real monthly spend'.
acceptance_test: A reader can trace, from the Canonical Workload box alone, the host count used in Table 4-1's Economic row, the sidebar's $87.6K–$306.6K range, the ~2.76M tokens-per-dollar figure, and the ~$0.0033/~$0.0029 owned per-request costs, and each of those four numbers recomputes from the same stated host count and the same stated utilization policy. No two of them may rest on different host counts.

page_hint: Ch 2, §1 Concept (decode paragraph); Ch 2 §3 Table 2-1 rows 'Decode: required bandwidth' and 'Decode: bandwidth verdict'; Ch 2 §3 'Decode bandwidth' bullet; Ch 2 §5 Common Mistakes bullet 2; Ch 2 §8 mini-case
quoted_clause: Decode: required bandwidth (TPOT ~25 ms) | 5.6 TB/s | 140 GB / 0.025 s (batch-1-equivalent weight-streaming model, before amortization) ... Decode: bandwidth verdict | bandwidth-bound | 5.6 > 3.35 → under the batch-1-equivalent model, a single H100 cannot meet the demand ... decode will be bandwidth-bound (a ~140 GB/token weight-read requiring ~5.6 TB/s sustained over each ~25 ms decode step)
observed: The chapter's headline regime claim is supported by comparing an *aggregate* model-wide traffic figure (140 GB/token) against a *single device's* capability (3.35 TB/s). That comparison does not describe the canonical deployment, which is 8×H100 with the model sharded by tensor parallelism. The chapter itself concedes the comparison is 'deliberately hypothetical' in §3, but then restates it without the hedge in the §8 mini-case ('decode will be bandwidth-bound (a ~140 GB/token weight-read requiring ~5.6 TB/s sustained over each ~25 ms decode step)') and in §5 Common Mistakes ('a single H100 cannot meet the decode bandwidth demand (5.6 TB/s vs 3.35 TB/s)'), where it is presented as a property of the canonical 8×H100 host. A reader can legitimately conclude that the canonical host cannot meet its 25 ms TPOT budget, which is false.
evidence: Per-GPU shard under TP=8: 70B/8 = 8.75B params/GPU = 17.5 GB FP16 per GPU per decode step. Required per-GPU rate at a 25 ms TPOT: 17.5 GB / 0.025 s = 700 GB/s = 21% of the 3.35 TB/s H100 peak — comfortably feasible at batch 1. The regime label 'bandwidth-bound' is nonetheless correct on the canonical host, but for a different reason: per GPU, weight-read time = 17.5/3350 = 5.22 ms per step while compute per step at batch B = B × 1.75e10 FLOP / 0.989e15 = B × 0.0177 ms, so the weight read binds until B ≈ 295. The book's printed 5.6 TB/s vs 3.35 TB/s comparison is an aggregate-vs-device mismatch that happens to reach the right regime label by an invalid route.
root_cause: The chapter's first-pass arithmetic was deliberately posed on a hypothetical single-device model (140 GB FP16 cannot fit on an 80 GB H100) and the resulting numbers were then reused as if they described the canonical multi-GPU host, without re-deriving the per-GPU quantities.
correction: Keep the aggregate illustration but (a) mark the mini-case and Common-Mistakes restatements with the same 'aggregate, hypothetical single-device' qualifier the §3 bullet carries, or replace them with the per-GPU derivation; and (b) add the canonical-host per-GPU numbers (17.5 GB/GPU/token → 700 GB/s at 25 ms; weight-read-bound until batch ≈ 295) so the reader can see the regime claim holds for the deployment the book actually sizes. The Common-Mistake bullet's real argument should be led with the residency fact (140 GB > 80 GB), which is unconditional, rather than the hypothetical bandwidth comparison.
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '5.6 TB/s' in Ch 2 is either explicitly labelled as an aggregate single-device hypothetical or is accompanied by the per-GPU shard figure (17.5 GB/GPU/token, 700 GB/s at 25 ms). A reader who checks the canonical 8×H100 host against the 25 ms TPOT budget finds the arithmetic shown, not just the verdict.

page_hint: Ch 2, §6 Architecture Consequence, second bullet ('With decode in the bandwidth-bound regime → optimization levers')
quoted_clause: continuous batching (vLLM, PagedAttention) to amortize weight reads across many tokens in flight, KV cache offloading to SSD or system memory, P/D (prefill/decode) disaggregation ... and higher-bandwidth memory and interconnect topologies (HBM3e memory per GPU; NVSwitch/NVLink for GPU-to-GPU communication)
observed: The optimization-lever list contradicts the chapter's own definitions two pages earlier. (a) 'continuous batching (vLLM, PagedAttention)' presents PagedAttention as part of the weight-read amortization mechanism, whereas the §1 vocabulary table defines PagedAttention as 'a memory-*allocation* scheme for the KV cache (splits it into fixed-size pages, cuts fragmentation/waste)' and 'not a way to *reduce* the amount of KV state' — it does not amortize weight reads. (b) 'KV cache offloading to SSD or system memory' is listed as a decode *bandwidth* lever, whereas the same table defines KV offloading as 'moving some KV state out of GPU HBM ... trading capacity against transfer latency' — it relieves memory *capacity* pressure and adds transfer latency; it does not raise HBM bandwidth. (c) NVSwitch/NVLink is a GPU-to-GPU interconnect, not a source of HBM bandwidth for weight streaming.
evidence: The book's own §1 table: 'PagedAttention | a memory-*allocation* scheme for the KV cache | not a way to *reduce* the amount of KV state'; 'KV offloading | moving some KV state out of GPU HBM (to host DRAM/SSD), trading capacity against transfer latency | not shrinking the state itself'. The §1 'discipline' paragraph also assigns each mechanism a distinct resource: 'KV quantization trades *capacity* for a small precision loss; prefix caching trades *prefill compute* for *cache residency*; continuous batching trades *latency* for *utilization*'. The §6 list collapses three of these.
root_cause: The lever list was written as a familiar-technology catalogue rather than as the resource-shifting table the chapter had already established, so the mechanism→resource mapping the chapter promises is not applied to the chapter's own examples.
correction: Rewrite the decode-lever bullet so each item names the resource it shifts and the resource it costs, in the same form as the §1 discipline paragraph: continuous batching → amortizes weight reads, trades per-request latency for utilization; PagedAttention → removes fragmentation waste, raises effective KV capacity, no effect on weight traffic; KV offloading → raises KV capacity headroom, adds transfer latency and PCIe/host-DRAM traffic; KV quantization → shrinks bytes per element, costs precision; P/D disaggregation → separates compute-bound and bandwidth-bound pools, costs duplicated residency and KV transfer. Drop NVSwitch/NVLink from the bandwidth list or restate it as a TP-communication lever.
acceptance_test: Each item in Ch 2 §6's lever lists maps to exactly one row of the §1 resource table and to exactly one row of the §1 vocabulary table, with no item appearing under two resources and no two items sharing a mechanism.

page_hint: Ch 4, §8 mini-case (prefill-throughput cross-check paragraph); Ch 4 §3 'Throughput per dollar' bullet
quoted_clause: ÷ ~19,800 tokens/s per host (the host's *sustained-planning* prefill rate, 8 × 2,472 tok/s at 35% MFU — a planning rate, not a ceiling: the peak-derived ceiling is ~56.5K tok/s; not a measured goodput)
observed: The per-GPU decomposition of the host's prefill rate is inconsistent with the tensor-parallel sharding the same book assumes. 2,472 tok/s is the rate of a *single GPU holding the whole 70B model* (0.35 × 989 TFLOPS ÷ 2 × 70e9 FLOP/token). Under TP=8 each GPU holds 1/8 of the weights (8.75B params → 1.75e10 FLOP/token) and therefore sustains ~19,780 tok/s of the *shared* token stream, not 2,472. Multiplying 8 × 2,472 happens to land on the correct host aggregate (19,776) only because the sharding is applied twice — once to FLOPs/token and once to the GPU count. The book uses 2,472 correctly elsewhere (Ch 4 §3: 'far above what a single H100 alone could sustain'), so the same number carries two incompatible meanings.
evidence: Per-GPU shard: 0.35 × 0.989e15 FLOP/s ÷ (2 × 8.75e9 FLOP/token) = 19,780 tok/s per GPU; all 8 GPUs process the same tokens under TP, so the host rate is 19,780 tok/s. Host peak: 8 × 0.989e15 ÷ 1.4e11 = 56,514 tok/s ✓ (the book's ~56.5K is right). Single-GPU-whole-model rate: 0.35 × 0.989e15 ÷ 1.4e11 = 2,472 tok/s ✓ (the book's number, but it is a whole-model-on-one-GPU figure, not a per-shard figure).
root_cause: The host rate was derived correctly at the aggregate level and then decomposed per-GPU by dividing by 8, without noticing that the aggregate already reflects the 8-way weight sharding.
correction: State the host rate directly with its derivation (8 × 0.989 PFLOPS × 35% MFU ÷ 1.4e11 FLOP/token ≈ 19,800 tok/s), and if a per-GPU figure is wanted, give the correct one (each of the 8 GPUs sustains ~19,800 tok/s of the shared token stream because each holds 1/8 of the weights) or explicitly label 2,472 tok/s as 'a single H100 holding the entire model'.
acceptance_test: The parenthetical '8 × 2,472 tok/s' is replaced by a derivation that a reader can reproduce from (a) the 8-way weight sharding and (b) the 35% MFU assumption, and the number 2,472 appears in the book with only one meaning.

page_hint: Ch 2, §3 'Scope of the single-host premise' paragraph vs §3 Table 2-1 and the 'Prefill FLOPs' bullet
quoted_clause: Throughout this chapter and the arithmetic chapters that follow, '1 host with 8×H100' is a **per-host / per-request feasibility** container: it asks whether one host can meet the per-request latency and memory SLO (TTFT 1.2 s, TPOT ~25 ms, KV residency) for a single in-flight request.

Every worked number in §3 is computed for a *single H100* (5.6 TB/s vs 3.35 TB/s; 1.19 PFLOPS vs 0.989 PFLOPS), and the chapter concludes that one H100 is insufficient. page_hint: Ch 1, §1 Concept, 'Attention' subsection, third paragraph
quoted_clause: That quadratic term is the single biggest reason context windows feel expensive, and it is the pivot for every optimization downstream (sparse/linear attention, KV caching, retrieval to keep context short).
observed: KV caching is listed as a downstream optimization of the quadratic attention term. It is not: the KV cache eliminates redundant *recomputation* of the prefix during decode; it does not reduce the quadratic pairwise work of a prefill pass at all (a full prefill still computes all L² position pairs). Listing it in that parenthetical invites the reader to believe that KV caching mitigates the quadratic cost — the exact misconception the surrounding paragraph is trying to prevent.
evidence: The same chapter's own KV-cache section states the cache 'is the reason "long conversations are expensive in memory, not just in compute"' — a memory effect, not a quadratic-compute effect. Ch 2 §1 likewise separates the two: the L² term is a prefill cost, while decode is linear-but-memory-growing.
root_cause: A list of 'things that address long context' was written where a list of 'things that reduce the quadratic term' was intended.
correction: Remove 'KV caching' from that parenthetical, or rephrase to distinguish the two families: 'sparse/linear attention and retrieval-to-keep-context-short reduce the quadratic term; KV caching removes redundant recomputation during decode and converts the cost into a memory-footprint problem (Ch 7).'
acceptance_test: A reader who asks 'does the KV cache reduce the quadratic attention cost?' finds an explicit 'no' in the text near the quadratic claim, not silence.

page_hint: Ch 4, §3 sidebar table 'what the ~$15,000 budget line is, and the 6–21-host workload comparison', 'Per 1K req' column and its footnote
quoted_clause: The *Per 1K req* column divides *Monthly* by the canonical request volume: **~6.24M active-hours requests/month** (10 rps × 3,600 s × 8 h × 260 workdays ÷ 12 = 6,240,000 ...)
observed: The 'Per 1K req' column divides a *peak-capacity* numerator (the 21-host always-on-at-peak row, $306,600) by an *average-volume* denominator (6.24M requests/month at the 10 rps average). The resulting ~$49.13/1K req is neither the cost of serving average traffic nor the cost of serving peak traffic; it is the cost of peak capacity amortized over average volume. The row labels ('always-on at peak', 'peak KV-screen fleet') do not carry that meaning, and the column header invites the reader to read it as a per-request cost at the stated traffic. The same mixing appears in the mini-case ('$306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K').
evidence: 6.24M requests/month is the 10 rps average volume (10 × 3600 × 8 × 260 ÷ 12 = 6,240,000 ✓). The 21-host row's monthly figure is peak-provisioned capacity ($306,600). At the 40 rps peak the monthly volume would be 24.96M, giving $306,600 ÷ 24,960K ≈ $12.28/1K req — half the printed number.
root_cause: A single 'Per 1K req' column was applied to rows whose numerators are priced at different operating points, without normalizing the denominator to match.
correction: Split the column into 'per 1K req @ average volume' and 'per 1K req @ peak volume', or add an explicit 'volume basis' column stating which request volume each row's numerator is paired with. If the intent is 'cost of peak capacity amortized over average volume', rename the column accordingly (e.g. 'peak-capacity cost per 1K avg-volume req').
acceptance_test: Every row in the sidebar table states the request volume its per-1K-req figure is divided by, and the peak row's figure is not readable as a per-request cost at the average traffic.

page_hint: Ch 2, Table 2-1 row 'Prefill: regime verdict'; Fig 2.2 caption
quoted_clause: arithmetic intensity ~9.2K FLOP/byte > ridge ~295 → on the compute-bound side of the roofline
observed: The stated prefill arithmetic intensity is not derived, and the value corresponds to counting weight bytes only: 2NL/W = 1.288e15 / 140e9 = 9,200 FLOP/byte. It omits the KV write traffic (24.1 GB at 9.2K tokens) and activation traffic. Including KV writes the intensity is 1.288e15 / (140e9 + 24.1e9) ≈ 7.9K FLOP/byte. The regime verdict is unchanged (both are far above the 295 ridge), but a reader who tries to reproduce the printed number from the book's own byte counts will not land on it.

root_cause: The intensity was computed from the dominant term without stating the approximation or the omitted terms.
correction: Show the derivation inline ('weight-traffic-only approximation: 2NL/W = 9,200 FLOP/byte; including the 24.1 GB of KV writes gives ≈7,900 — both far above the 295 ridge') so the number is reproducible and its approximation is explicit.
acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce the printed prefill intensity from the book's own FLOP and byte figures, or the book states which byte terms are excluded.

page_hint: Ch 3, §4 Measurement, item 2
quoted_clause: Tools such as `torch.profiler` can count active parameters, but this is an empirical measurement, not a first-party spec.
observed: torch.profiler does not count active parameters; it records operator-level events, from which FLOP counts (and hence an inferred active-parameter figure) can be derived only with additional instrumentation and per-op shape analysis. As written, the sentence tells the reader to reach for a tool that does not do what is claimed.
evidence: torch.profiler exposes operator timings and (with FLOP-count instrumentation) per-op FLOPs; active-parameter counts are obtained by summing the shapes of the executed matmuls, or by instrumenting the MoE router's expert selection.
root_cause: Tool capability stated more strongly than the tool provides.
correction: Rewrite as: 'Runtime measurement. Profile the executed matmul shapes (e.g. torch.profiler with FLOP counting, or a router hook that records the selected experts per token) and infer the active-parameter count from the shapes actually executed. This is an empirical measurement, not a first-party spec.'
acceptance_test: The named tool is described with a capability it actually has, and the sentence tells the reader what to do with the profile output.

page_hint: Ch 1, §5 Common Mistakes, first bullet

The range is plausible for code and CJK text but is workload- and tokenizer-dependent, and 'routinely' is a strong frequency claim.

page_hint: Ch 2, §6 Architecture Consequence, decode-lever bullet, final clause
quoted_clause: higher-bandwidth memory and interconnect topologies (HBM3e memory per GPU; NVSwitch/NVLink for GPU-to-GPU communication)
observed: NVSwitch/NVLink is listed as a lever for decode's HBM-bandwidth constraint. GPU-to-GPU interconnect does not supply HBM bandwidth to a weight-streaming kernel; it carries tensor-parallel activations and all-reduce traffic, and it *adds* traffic to the critical path. Listing it under 'higher-bandwidth memory' conflates the interconnect resource with the memory-bandwidth resource — the same conflation the chapter's own resource table separates ('memory bandwidth | bytes/s | how fast data can move' vs 'interconnect bandwidth/latency | bytes/s, delay | cross-GPU / cross-host movement').
evidence: Ch 2 §1 resource table distinguishes the two rows; Ch 2 §3's decode bullet separately notes that on a TP deployment 'each GPU streams only its shard against its own 3.35 TB/s, plus communication overhead' — i.e. the interconnect is a cost, not a source of bandwidth.
root_cause: The lever list mixes 'things that increase bandwidth' with 'things that increase bandwidth *and* add communication', without the resource labels the chapter promises.
correction: Split the clause: 'higher-bandwidth memory (HBM3e per GPU) raises the decode weight-read ceiling; higher-bandwidth interconnect (NVLink/NVSwitch) reduces the *cost* of tensor-parallel sharding but does not raise HBM bandwidth for weight streaming.'
acceptance_test: Every lever in Ch 2 §6 is assigned to exactly one row of the §1 resource table, and no interconnect item appears under 'memory bandwidth'.

page_hint: Ch 6 §3 'Reading Telemetry Into a Decision'; Ch 6 §6 bullet 2; Ch 6 §8 mini-case
quoted_clause: low prefix-cache hit means many independent 9.2K prefixes are being prefill-processed from scratch on the ~40 rps peak ... The decision: enable prefix / RadixAttention-style caching (SGLang) or Automatic Prefix Caching (vLLM) so shared retrieved-context prefixes are reused instead of re-prefilled, cutting effective prefill FLOPs and TTFT. | Repeat-prefix RAG ⇒ enable prefix caching (RadixAttention/APC), which turns repeated 9.2K prefills into cached lookups and defends the p95 TTFT against the 40 rps peaks. | The fix is not "buy GPUs immediately" — it is to enable prefix caching to collapse the repeated prefills
observed: The chapter treats the canonical RAG workload's 9.2K input as a repeat prefix that prefix caching can reuse. In the canonical workload (Ch 4, Table 4-2) the 9.2K input is 1,200 prompt + 8K *retrieved* context. The retrieved 8K is selected per query from the corpus and is therefore query-specific; the only cross-request shared prefix is the ~1,200-token system prompt. Prefix caching can therefore remove at most ~13% of the prefill work (1,200/9,200), not the 9.2K. The chapter's own framing 'Repeat-prefix RAG' is false for a standard RAG system as characterized.
evidence: Canonical workload composition (Ch 5 §3, Ch 7 §3): 1,200 prompt + 8,000 retrieved = 9,200 input. Prefix-cache reuse requires byte-identical token prefixes; retrieved chunks differ per query by construction. Ch 6's own arithmetic (40 rps × 1.29 PFLOP = 52 PFLOP/s) is computed on the full 9.2K, so the proposed fix cannot remove the demand the same paragraph quantifies.
root_cause: Conflation of 'shared system prompt' with 'shared retrieved context' — a mechanism-level error about what prefix caching actually keys on, propagated into a recommended architecture action.
correction: Rewrite the three passages to state that APC/RadixAttention reuse requires a byte-identical prefix; in the canonical workload that is the ~1,200-token system prompt (≈13% of prefill FLOPs), so prefix caching is a partial mitigation, not the fix for the 40 rps prefill queue. If the intended workload has a shared document prefix (e.g. a fixed corpus preamble), say so explicitly and add it to the canonical workload table. Replace 'Repeat-prefix RAG' with a conditional ('RAG with a shared system-prompt prefix, or with repeated document blocks').
acceptance_test: A reader can answer: 'In the canonical workload, what fraction of the 9.2K prefill can prefix caching actually reuse, and why?' Answer: ~1,200/9,200 ≈ 13% (the system prompt), because the 8K retrieved block is query-specific. No sentence in Ch 6 asserts that 9.2K prefills become cache lookups.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), final HYPOTHESIS paragraph
quoted_clause: The decision hinges on whether the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain (reports span a few to ~15%, domain- and corpus-specific — §3) translates into sufficient answer-quality improvement to justify the 2×FLOP cost
observed: The decision under discussion is mpnet-base-v2 (768-dim) vs MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-dim). The FLOP ratio between those two models is 14.08 / 2.94 = 4.79×, not 2×. The '2×' figure belongs to the same-family dimension-reduction case mentioned in the same parenthetical, which is a different comparison.
evidence: Table 5-1 rows: 2 × 110M × 64 = 14.08 GFLOP; 2 × 23M × 64 = 2.94 GFLOP. Ratio = 4.79. The paragraph's own parenthetical distinguishes 'a cross-model difference, not a dim-only sweep' from 'a same-family 384-dim variant is the ~2× case', so the closing '2×FLOP cost' contradicts the comparison actually being made.
root_cause: The same-family '2×' figure was carried into a sentence whose subject is the cross-model comparison.
correction: Replace 'the 2×FLOP cost' with 'the ~4.8×FLOP cost (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP per 64-token query, Table 5-1)' for the mpnet-vs-MiniLM decision, and keep the ~2× figure only where the same-family dimension sweep is the subject.
acceptance_test: Every FLOP ratio quoted in §3(a) can be reproduced from Table 5-1's own rows, and the ratio attached to the mpnet-vs-MiniLM decision equals 4.79 (rounded), not 2.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), first HYPOTHESIS paragraph
quoted_clause: reducing the embedding dimension may trade retrieval quality for lower storage and compute — e.g. a 384-dim variant of the same model family can cost roughly half the FLOPs and index storage of a 768-dim one
observed: Reducing the output dimension of a same-family embedding model (e.g. truncating or re-projecting all-mpnet-base-v2 to 384 dims) halves the *index storage* but does not halve the encoder FLOPs: the transformer body and its projections are unchanged, and only the final projection head shrinks (768×384 vs 768×768, i.e. ~0.09M of ~110M parameters). The claim that a same-family dimension reduction halves compute is incorrect.
evidence: Encoder FLOPs are set by the parameter count of the body (2 × params × L); the output projection is 768×768 = 0.59M of 110M params for mpnet. Halving the output dimension changes ~0.3M params, i.e. ~0.3% of the FLOPs, not 50%.
root_cause: Storage-per-vector reasoning was transferred to compute-per-query reasoning without checking which parameters the dimension actually controls.
correction: Split the claim: 'a 384-dim variant of the same family halves index storage (and the projection head's FLOPs, which are negligible) but leaves the encoder's compute essentially unchanged; the ~2× compute reduction quoted for MiniLM is a cross-model difference (smaller body), not a dimension effect.'
acceptance_test: The reader can state which of {storage, encoder FLOPs, projection FLOPs} a same-family dimension reduction changes and by how much; no sentence claims a same-family dim reduction halves encoder compute.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a), Table 5-1 footnote and HYPOTHESIS paragraph
quoted_clause: FLOPs per embedding = 2 × params × L at a 64-token query (L = 64); the value scales linearly with query length, so the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio (bge-large ≈ 3× mpnet).
observed: The 2 × params × L rule multiplies every parameter by the sequence length, but a token-embedding table is a lookup, not a per-position matmul. The share of parameters that are embedding-table entries differs sharply across the three models (MiniLM-L6-v2: 30,522 × 384 ≈ 11.7M of ~23M ≈ 51%; mpnet-base-v2: 30,522 × 768 ≈ 23.4M of ~110M ≈ 21%; bge-large-en: 30,522 × 1,024 ≈ 31.3M of ~335M ≈ 9%). The rule therefore overstates compute for MiniLM far more than for the others, so the claim that the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio does not hold for the compute these models actually perform.
evidence: MiniLM-L6-v2: 22.7M params, of which the word-embedding matrix is 11.7M. Body-only params ≈ 11M vs mpnet body-only ≈ 86.6M — a ~7.9× ratio, not the 4.8× implied by total parameters. The chapter's incremental-cost figure (11.1 GFLOP) and the CPU/GPU latency estimates (56–370 ms / 1.1 ms) inherit this distortion.
root_cause: A transformer-forward proxy (2 × N × L) was applied to encoder-only models whose largest parameter block is a lookup table, without noting the exception.
correction: State the proxy's scope explicitly: '2 × params × L treats the token-embedding table as a per-position matmul; for encoder-only models this overstates compute, and the overstatement is largest for the smallest model (MiniLM's table is ~half its parameters). The cross-model ratios below are therefore upper bounds on the true compute ratio.' Optionally give body-only parameter counts in the table.
acceptance_test: The table footnote states the proxy's scope and its direction of error; the ratio claim is either corrected to a body-parameter ratio or explicitly labelled as an upper bound.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(a) HYPOTHESIS paragraph and Takeaway; Ch 5 §7 first bullet
quoted_clause: Any observed quality-vs-dimension relationship (reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference) is domain- and corpus-specific and must be validated on the target corpus. | It places the workload in the quality-positive regime without introducing per-request latency that threatens the TTFT SLO. | Early evidence suggests 768 dim is a sweet spot
observed: The chapter's central recommendation (768-dim all-mpnet-base-v2) rests on an unsourced empirical claim ('reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference'; 'Early evidence suggests 768 dim is a sweet spot') with no citation, while the *bge-large-en* option is rejected precisely because 'its quality gain over all-mpnet-base-v2 is not quantified for this model pair'. The evidentiary standard is applied asymmetrically: an unquantified gain disqualifies one candidate but supports the recommendation of another. The phrase 'quality-positive regime' is also undefined.
evidence: No reference is attached to the ~15% MAP figure or to the '768 dim is a sweet spot' statement anywhere in the chunk, while the chapter elsewhere attaches [1P]/[2°] provenance to every other empirical claim (e.g. the 30–40% MFU range in Ch 8).
root_cause: The recommendation was written before the evidence was sourced, and the rejection criterion was applied only to the candidate that was being dropped.
correction: Either (a) cite the MAP studies (with corpus, query set, and metric definition) and label them [2°][FACT], or (b) restate the recommendation as conditional: '768-dim is the default choice pending a target-corpus evaluation; the decision rule is Δanswer-quality per unit of added latency, and the ~15% figure is an unverified prior.' Apply the same 'must be quantified' test to all three candidates, and define or delete 'quality-positive regime'.
acceptance_test: Every empirical quality claim in Ch 5 carries a source and a provenance label, and the same quantification test is visibly applied to the recommended candidate as to the rejected one.

page_hint: Ch 5 §2 Mental Model; compare Ch 8 §1 'Three different bounds' callout and Ch 8 §3 host-screen table
quoted_clause: If the workload is input-heavy (9.2K average input, 300-token output, ~30× more input than output), the system is memory‑capacity‑bound (KV residency) and prefill‑dominated — prefill itself sits in the compute‑bound regime (Ch 2).
observed: The chapter asserts the canonical system is memory-capacity-bound. The book's own fleet screens contradict this: Ch 8's three-case table gives a KV-residency/Little's-Law screen of 21 hosts at peak against a compute screen of 19 hosts under case (i) and 21 under case (iii) — i.e. the KV screen binds under the linear-only case, and the compute screen binds only under case (ii). Ch 8's callout also states explicitly: 'Input-heavy does not by itself mean "memory-bound" — it tends to raise prefill compute and KV-capacity pressure, two distinct effects.' Ch 5 asserts one of the two effects as the system's regime without the qualification.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'the capacity floor is the max of the named screens — 21 hosts under case (i), 22 under case (ii)'; Ch 8 §1: 'The canonical RAG workload illustrates all three without overlap' — a claim that is itself in tension with the 21-vs-19 screen ordering.
root_cause: A regime label was asserted in Ch 5 before the screens that determine the binding constraint were derived in Ch 8, and the two chapters were not reconciled.
correction: Rewrite as: 'an input-heavy workload raises both prefill compute demand and KV-capacity pressure; which binds is decided by the screens in Ch 8 (KV residency binds under the linear-only FLOP case, compute under the conservative case).' Remove 'the system is memory-capacity-bound' as a flat characterization.
acceptance_test: Ch 5's regime statement is consistent with Ch 8's screen ordering, and no chapter asserts a single binding regime for the canonical workload without naming the FLOP-counting case.

page_hint: Ch 5 §5 Common Mistakes, third bullet
quoted_clause: The break-even analysis (the parametric $Q^*$ in §5.3) shows that for most enterprise RAG workloads, the RAG + guardrails paradigm dominates on TCO.
observed: The break-even analysis defines a formula with three unmeasured inputs; it does not 'show' anything about 'most enterprise RAG workloads'. This directly contradicts §3(c) ('The economic comparison should be framed parametrically, not with a single number'), the §3(c) Takeaway ('the break-even ΔQ/Q of §5.3 is parametric here, not measured for this workload') and §7 ('Any quoted break-even volume is a derived scenario value').
evidence: Three statements in the same chapter contradict the Common Mistakes bullet; the chapter's own §7 lists the break-even as [HYPOTHESIS].
root_cause: A summary bullet was written from the chapter's conclusion rather than from its evidence, and the chapter's own hedging was not carried into it.
correction: Rewrite: 'The parametric $Q^*$ in §5.3 shows *how* to decide — RAG + guardrails dominates below the break-even volume, fine-tuning may dominate above it — but the break-even is workload- and domain-specific and must be measured before either paradigm is declared dominant.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 5 asserts a general dominance result for 'most enterprise RAG workloads' without a measured ΔQ and query volume.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(c), $Q^*$ equation and surrounding paragraph
quoted_clause: Q^* = (C_train + C_weights-extra) / (ΔQ · value per corrected query) ... Below $Q^*$, RAG + guardrails is economically dominant because the fine-tuning cost is spread over too few queries to be repaid; above it, fine-tuning may recover its upfront cost through quality gain.
observed: The break-even model compares only the fine-tuning side's one-time and carry costs against a quality uplift. It omits the recurring per-query cost difference between the two paradigms, which the chapter itself identifies: RAG pays retrieval plus a 9.2K-token prefill per query (~1.08 s of prefill on the canonical host), while the fine-tuned model 'uses the fine-tuned weights without a retrieval step, or with a much shorter retrieved context'. A paradigm that removes 9.2K of prefill per query has a large recurring saving that the formula cannot see, so the formula can predict the wrong direction of the break-even.
evidence: Ch 5 §3(c) states the fine-tuned model may run 'with a much shorter retrieved context'; Ch 5 §3(b) prices the canonical prefill at ~1.08 s per request on the 8×H100 host. Neither quantity appears in $Q^*$.
root_cause: The break-even was modelled as a pure fixed-cost-amortization problem, omitting the variable-cost term that the chapter's own paradigm description introduces.
correction: Extend the model to a total-cost-per-query comparison: TCO_RAG(Q) = Q·(c_retrieval + c_prefill_9.2K + c_decode) + C_RAG; TCO_FT(Q) = Q·(c_prefill_short + c_decode) + C_train + C_weights-extra; then define Q* as the crossing point. State explicitly that the current formula is a lower bound on the fine-tuning case because it omits the recurring prefill saving.
acceptance_test: The break-even discussion accounts for the per-query prefill/retrieval cost of both paradigms, and the reader can say which term the original formula omitted and in which direction it biases the result.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b), 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included' paragraph vs the 'Economics unit note'
quoted_clause: But it is only ~13% of the wall-clock time (1.08 s prefill vs 7.5 s decode) ... The ~50 tok/s here (this worked example's low-batch decode point, ~20 ms/token — the canonical batch-1 rate at 25 ms/token is ~40 tok/s, Ch 2)
observed: The same worked example uses two different decode rates without reconciling them in the paragraph that needs one: the economics use 50 tok/s (20 ms/token), while the wall-clock split uses 7.5 s of decode, which is 300 tokens at the canonical 25 ms/token (40 tok/s). The 8.6 s service time used in Ch 17's Little's-Law screen (λ·W ≈ 344) is consistent with 1.08 + 7.5 = 8.58 s, i.e. with 25 ms/token — so the wall-clock split is on the canonical basis while the economics are on a different, faster basis. At 20 ms/token the decode leg is 6.0 s and the prefill share of wall-clock is ~15%, not ~13%.
root_cause: Two operating points (canonical batch-1 and the illustrative low-batch point) coexist in one worked example, and the paragraph that mixes them does not say which it uses.
correction: State the decode rate explicitly in the wall-clock paragraph ('at the canonical 25 ms/token, 300 output tokens take 7.5 s, giving the 8.6 s service time used in Ch 17'), and either use the same 25 ms/token in the economics or add a one-line note that the 50 tok/s point is a separate illustrative operating point whose service time would be 1.08 + 6.0 = 7.1 s.
acceptance_test: Every decode rate quoted in Ch 5 §3(b) is labelled with its operating point, and the wall-clock split can be reconciled with the 8.6 s service time used in Ch 17.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b) ILLUSTRATIVE paragraph; compare Ch 6 §3 and Ch 4 canonical SLO
quoted_clause: Adding retrieval (~120 ms) puts the full TTFT (retrieval + prefill) at ~1.20 s, i.e. at the 1.2 s SLO line with no prefill-side margin; the real margin is the p95 ≤ 2 s target.
observed: The 1.2 s figure is the internal design budget for TTFT; the SLO is stated at p95 ≤ 2 s (Ch 4 Table 4-2, Ch 6 §3: 'the SLO itself is stated at p95'). Calling 1.2 s 'the 1.2 s SLO line' conflates the design budget with the SLO and, read literally, asserts that the system is exactly at its SLO with zero margin — when in fact the p95 SLO has ~0.8 s of margin. The same paragraph also says the prefill 'leaves ~0.12 s of headroom against the 1.2 s budget *for prefill alone*', although the 1.2 s budget is not a prefill-only budget (it includes retrieval).
evidence: Ch 6 §3: 'We budget TTFT ≤ 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08 s) with a p95 ≤ 2 s'; Ch 6 §3 also: 'the SLO itself is stated at p95'. Ch 5 §8 mini-case: 'The prefill TTFT of ~1.08 s plus retrieval (~120 ms) sits at the 1.2 s TTFT budget, with the p95 ≤ 2 s SLO giving the real margin' — the mini-case gets this right, so the chapter is internally inconsistent.
root_cause: Budget and SLO terminology drifted; the design budget was relabelled as an SLO in one paragraph.
correction: Use 'design budget' for 1.2 s and 'SLO' only for p95 ≤ 2 s throughout Ch 5. Rewrite the sentence as: 'the full TTFT (retrieval + prefill) reaches ~1.20 s, exactly consuming the 1.2 s design budget; the p95 ≤ 2 s SLO remains the binding acceptance criterion.' Delete 'for prefill alone'.
acceptance_test: In Ch 5, every occurrence of 'SLO' refers to the p95 ≤ 2 s / p95 ≤ 35 ms targets, and 1.2 s / 25 ms are consistently called budgets or design points.

page_hint: Ch 6 §3 'Goodput vs Raw Throughput'
quoted_clause: The extra 20 tok/s are produced, but they land in the tail that misses the SLO, so goodput does not grow. Raw throughput is up 40%; **goodput** (tokens that met the SLO) is effectively unchanged *in this case*
observed: The headline claim ('goodput does not grow') is asserted with no evidence: a p95 TTFT shift from 1.8 s to 2.3 s is a percentile statement and says nothing about which requests carry the extra tokens. The chapter then immediately supplies a counterexample in which goodput rises 37% (48 → 65.8), and the general relation it gives (goodput = raw_rate × compliant_fraction) contradicts the headline in the common case. The reader is left with 'goodput does not grow' as the memorable conclusion even though the arithmetic shown two sentences later says otherwise.
evidence: 50 × 0.96 = 48 vs 70 × 0.94 = 65.8 (the chapter's own numbers). For goodput to be unchanged, the compliant fraction must fall from 96% to 96 × 50/70 = 68.6% — a 27-point drop, not the 2-point drop illustrated.
root_cause: A rhetorical example was written first ('bigger batch, worse goodput') and the quantitative treatment that refutes it was appended without reconciling the two.
correction: Restructure: state the general relation first (goodput = raw_rate × compliant_fraction), then give the two regimes as worked instances — (i) compliant fraction falls proportionally (96% → 68.6%): goodput flat at 48; (ii) compliant fraction falls only slightly (96% → 94%): goodput rises to 65.8 despite the p95 breach. Then state the lesson: a p95 breach is a configuration-level signal; goodput must be computed from the compliant fraction, and whether a given batching change helps depends on where the extra tokens land.
acceptance_test: The goodput section's headline claim is derivable from the relation the section itself states, and the two numeric instances are labelled as distinct regimes rather than one being presented as the general case.

page_hint: Ch 6 Fig 6.2 caption
quoted_clause: Fig 6.2 — Request-latency distribution: the mean looks healthy while a 1% tail at ~5 s breaches the 2 s SLO.
observed: The caption states that the tail 'breaches the 2 s SLO'. The SLO is stated at p95 (≤ 2 s), and the sample's p95 is ≈ 0.99 s — the SLO is comfortably met. What the 5 s stragglers breach is the per-request 2 s threshold, not the p95 SLO. The body text handles this correctly ('Under the canonical p95 TTFT SLO of ≤ 2 s, even this sample's p99 (≈ 1.33 s) still looks healthy'), so the caption and the body make different claims about the same figure. A reader who reads only the caption will conclude the system is in SLO violation.
evidence: Sample percentiles stated in the body: p50 ≈ 0.80, p90 ≈ 0.94, p95 ≈ 0.99, p99 ≈ 1.33 s. p95 = 0.99 s < 2 s ⇒ the p95 SLO is met; 1% of requests exceed 2 s.
root_cause: The caption was written to describe the shaded region (request-level threshold violations) and reused the word 'breaches', which the body reserves for the percentile SLO.
correction: Rewrite the caption's first clause: 'the mean looks healthy and the p95 SLO is met, while 1% of requests exceed the 2 s TTFT threshold — a tail that a p95 SLO does not surface.' Keep the existing caveat sentence about the shading.
acceptance_test: The Fig 6.2 caption and the §3 body agree on whether the p95 SLO is met; the caption distinguishes 'request exceeds the 2 s threshold' from 'p95 SLO breached'.

page_hint: Ch 6 §3 'Reading Telemetry Into a Decision'
quoted_clause: aggregate prefill demand at the 40 rps peak is 40 × 1.29 ≈ 52 PFLOP/s vs the 8×H100 aggregate ~7.9 PFLOPS, ~6.5× oversubscribed, so the prefill queue grows until backpressure or prefix caching intervenes
observed: The oversubscription is computed against the host's *peak* dense FP16 aggregate (8 × 0.989 = 7.91 PFLOPS) rather than the sustained rate the book uses everywhere else (8 × 0.989 × 0.35 = 2.7692 PFLOP/s, Ch 8 §3). Against the sustained rate the oversubscription is ~18.6×, not ~6.5×. Ch 8's own peak-rate screen (19 hosts at 40 rps) is consistent with the sustained figure, so Ch 6's number is inconsistent with the book's own fleet arithmetic and materially understates the pressure the paragraph describes.
evidence: 51.6 PFLOP/s ÷ 7.912 PFLOPS = 6.52×; 51.6 ÷ 2.7692 = 18.6×. Ch 8 §3: 'At the peak 40 rps (368,000 tokens/s) the same arithmetic gives ~18.6 → 19 hosts under case (i)'.
root_cause: A peak-vs-sustained scope slip: the chapter reached for the datasheet peak because it was the number already quoted in the same chapter (Table 6-1), without applying the book's own sustained-MFU convention.
correction: Use the sustained rate: 'aggregate prefill demand at the 40 rps peak is 40 × 1.29 ≈ 52 PFLOP/s against the 8×H100 sustained prefill capacity of ~2.77 PFLOP/s (35% MFU, Ch 8) — roughly 19× oversubscribed, consistent with Ch 8's 19-host screen at this peak.' If the peak figure is retained for contrast, label it explicitly as the theoretical ceiling.
acceptance_test: Every oversubscription or capacity ratio in Ch 6 states whether it is computed against peak or sustained capacity, and the value agrees with Ch 8's host screen for the same operating point.

page_hint: Ch 6 §6 bullet 3; Ch 7 §7 third bullet
quoted_clause: And vLLM KV-offloading (its own 2026-01-08 blog [S7][1P][FACT]) cuts TTFT by 2–22× in a particular warm-cache-hit/reuse benchmark, not a generic cold-cache improvement — both are memory-layer fixes the telemetry would call for when KV occupancy nears capacity.
observed: The mechanism is not explained, and the framing is counterintuitive enough to mislead: moving KV out of HBM adds a PCIe/host transfer on the critical path, so offloading cannot by itself reduce TTFT. The 2–22× TTFT reduction must come from the *reuse* that a larger (off-host) cache makes possible — i.e. the same mechanism as prefix caching, not offloading per se. The chapter presents it as a memory-layer fix whose headline benefit is TTFT, and Ch 7 §7 repeats the 2–22× figure without the mechanism.
evidence: Ch 7 §7 asks: 'Whether per-request KV caching can be partially offloaded to CPU DRAM during decode without TTFT impact' — offloading during decode affects inter-token latency, not TTFT, so the question conflates the two latency components as well.
correction: State the mechanism explicitly: 'KV offloading trades HBM capacity for transfer latency; the reported 2–22× TTFT reduction comes from the cross-request reuse that a host-resident cache enables (warm prefix hits), not from the offload itself. Cold-cache TTFT is unchanged or worse, and decode ITL pays the transfer cost.' In Ch 7 §7, reframe the open question around ITL/throughput at concurrency > 1 rather than TTFT.
acceptance_test: A reader can answer 'does moving KV to host DRAM make TTFT faster, and if not, where does the reported TTFT reduction come from?' without consulting another chapter.

page_hint: Ch 6 §6 bullet 1
quoted_clause: Bandwidth-bound decode + compute-bound prefill ⇒ P/D disaggregation (Splitwise/DistServe/Mooncake) is the remedy at scale, because squeezing both regimes from one resource pool fights itself. [S4][1P][FACT]
observed: The recommendation is presented as a direct consequence of the regime split, with no accounting of the cost disaggregation introduces: the prefill instance must hand the KV cache (or the hidden states) to the decode instance over the network, so the KV bytes that were resident in HBM become network traffic. At the canonical 9.2K context that is ~24.1 GB per request of KV to transfer, which is a first-order term against a ~1.2 s TTFT budget and a ~25 ms/token TPOT budget. The chapter's own §3 warns that regime classification is operating-point dependent, yet the consequence is stated unconditionally.
evidence: Ch 7 §3: 9,200 tokens × 2.62 MB = 24.1 GB of KV per request (FP16, full-MHA). Ch 6 §3: 'the same hardware, the same model — the boundary flips between prefill and decode' and '(This is an operating-point property, not an identity...)'.
root_cause: The consequence was derived from the regime split alone, without the transfer term that the regime split creates; the chapter's own operating-point caveat was not carried into the recommendation.
correction: Add the cost side: 'Disaggregation converts the KV residency problem into a KV transfer problem: ~24.1 GB per request at the canonical 9.2K context must cross the interconnect, so the design is viable only when the interconnect can sustain the transfer within the TTFT/TPOT budget and when the pool split is large enough to amortize it. The regime split is a necessary, not sufficient, condition.' Also state the operating-point dependence of the premise.
acceptance_test: The P/D bullet names the KV-transfer cost, quantifies it against the canonical context, and states the conditions under which disaggregation is and is not worth it.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph following the host-count table; compare Ch 8 §1 'Three different bounds' callout
quoted_clause: This rough sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale — the compute requirement is the primary constraint, and memory bandwidth (HBM at 3.35 TB/s per H100) is sufficient to keep the compute fed if the kernel is efficient.
observed: The chapter's own screen table, printed a few lines earlier, shows the opposite ordering under the linear-only case: the KV-residency/Little's-Law screen gives 21 hosts at peak while the compute screen gives 19 hosts under case (i) and 21 under case (iii). The compute screen binds only under case (ii) (22 hosts). So 'the compute requirement is the primary constraint' is true only under the conservative FLOP-counting case, and the sentence is stated unconditionally. The §1 callout's claim that the canonical workload 'illustrates all three without overlap' is in the same tension.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'the capacity floor is the max of the named screens — 21 hosts under case (i), 22 under case (ii)'; the KV screen is ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts.
root_cause: A summary sentence written from the roofline argument (prefill is compute-bound) without reconciling it against the fleet screens derived in the same section.
correction: Rewrite: 'This sizing illustrates that prefill is FLOP-bound at this scale — its arithmetic intensity (~9,200 FLOP/byte) is far above the ridge, so HBM bandwidth is sufficient to keep the compute fed. Whether prefill *compute* or KV *residency* is the binding fleet constraint is decided by the screens above: KV residency binds under cases (i) and (iii), compute under case (ii).' Amend the §1 callout's 'without overlap' to 'with the binding constraint depending on the FLOP-counting case'.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 8 asserts that compute is the primary fleet constraint without naming the FLOP-counting case under which that holds.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3 'Scope' note; Ch 6 §8 mini-case; Ch 5 §3(b)
quoted_clause: Scope. "1 host with 8×H100" here is a **per-host / per-request** feasibility container (does one host meet one request's latency and memory SLO). It is **not** a claim that one host absorbs the 40 rps peak arrival rate
observed: The Scope note disclaims only the peak rate. The canonical workload's *average* rate is ~10 rps, and the chapter's own arithmetic shows one host is insufficient there too: 92,000 prefill tokens/s ÷ 19,800 tokens/s per host ≈ 4.6 → ~5 hosts, and Ch 17's KV-residency screen at 10 rps (λ·W = 10 × 8.6 = 86 in-flight; 86/17 ≈ 5.1 → 6 hosts) agrees. Ch 6's mini-case nevertheless says 'The architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point', and Ch 5's worked example treats the single 8×H100 host as the serving configuration for the workload. The canonical scenario therefore reads as 'one host serves the workload' in at least three places while the book's own screens say five to six hosts at the average rate.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'n_hosts = 92,000/19,800 ≈ 4.6 → ~5 hosts'. Ch 8 §3 Scope note addresses only the 40 rps peak. Ch 6 §8: 'memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point'.
root_cause: The canonical scenario's '1 host' was reinterpreted locally as a per-request container in Ch 8 but never re-labelled in Ch 4's table or in the chapters that reuse it, so the ambiguity propagates.
correction: Extend the Scope note to the average rate ('one host does not absorb the 10 rps average either: the prefill screen alone needs ~5 hosts'), and re-label the canonical row in Ch 4 Table 4-2 as 'per-request feasibility container (1 host of 8×H100); fleet sizing in Ch 17'. Adjust Ch 6's mini-case wording so 'sane at the 10 rps design point' refers to the per-host resource envelope, not to the fleet.
acceptance_test: A reader who reads only Ch 4's canonical table and Ch 6's mini-case cannot conclude that a single 8×H100 host serves the canonical workload at 10 rps.

page_hint: Ch 8 §5 Common Mistakes, second bullet; compare Ch 8 §3 and Ch 6 §3
quoted_clause: Treating prefill and decode as having the same FLOP/byte profile. Prefill reads the full context once and is FLOP-bound; decode re-reads weights per token and is memory-bound.
observed: The Common Mistakes section states the two regimes unconditionally, which is the exact universal framing the rest of the book carefully avoids. Ch 8 §3 qualifies prefill as 'compute-bound at the canonical long-prompt operating point' and decode as 'memory-bound at low batch', and Ch 6 §3 adds '(This is an operating-point property, not an identity: at high batch decode climbs the intensity slope and can become compute-bound.)' The summary bullet drops both qualifiers, and a reader who consults only the Common Mistakes list will carry the universal version.
evidence: Ch 8 §3: 'at batch=32 the effective intensity is ~32 FLOP/byte, still ~9× below the 295 ridge'; 'decode stays bandwidth-bound at every batch size' only after the KV term is included; Ch 6 §3: 'the same hardware, the same model — the boundary flips between prefill and decode'.
root_cause: The Common Mistakes bullets were written as slogans rather than as compressed versions of the chapter's qualified findings.
correction: Rewrite: 'Treating prefill and decode as having the same FLOP/byte profile. At the canonical operating point prefill is compute-bound (intensity ~9,200 FLOP/byte, far above the ~295 ridge) and low-batch decode is bandwidth-bound (~1 FLOP/byte) — but both are operating-point properties: decode's intensity rises with batch, and prefill's falls as context shortens.'
acceptance_test: Every regime statement in Ch 8's Common Mistakes carries the same operating-point qualifier as the corresponding statement in §3.

page_hint: Ch 8 §4 Measurement, item 3
quoted_clause: GB200: higher on both terms (dense BF16 peak 4,500 TFLOPS = 2× B200's 2,250, over 16 TB/s HBM3e → 4,500 ÷ 16 ≈ 281 FLOP/byte, just below H100's ~295 — its 4.8× bandwidth advantage slightly outpaces its 4.5× compute advantage)
observed: The ridge value (281 FLOP/byte) is correct, but the granularity is unstated: 4,500 TFLOPS and 16 TB/s are both *per GB200 superchip* (two GPUs), while H100's 989 TFLOPS and 3.35 TB/s are per GPU. A reader can easily infer that a GB200 GPU has 16 TB/s of HBM3e (it does not; B200 has 8 TB/s per GPU) and that GB200 has 4,500 TFLOPS per GPU (it does not; 2,250 per GPU). The '4.8× bandwidth advantage' and '4.5× compute advantage' are likewise superchip-vs-GPU comparisons presented as if they were like-for-like.
evidence: B200 dense BF16 = 2,250 TFLOPS/GPU and 8 TB/s HBM3e/GPU; GB200 superchip = 2 GPUs → 4,500 TFLOPS and 16 TB/s. The ridge ratio is granularity-invariant (4,500/16 = 281.25 either way), so only the labelling is at issue.
root_cause: Per-part and per-GPU figures were mixed in a hardware-comparison sentence without a granularity marker.
correction: Add the granularity: 'GB200 superchip (2 GPUs): 4,500 TFLOPS dense BF16 and 16 TB/s HBM3e → 281 FLOP/byte; equivalently per GPU, 2,250 TFLOPS ÷ 8 TB/s = 281 FLOP/byte — the ridge is granularity-invariant.' Restate the advantage factors as per-GPU (2.28× compute, 2.39× bandwidth) or as superchip-vs-GPU with the basis named.
acceptance_test: Every hardware figure in the ridge comparison carries its granularity (per GPU / per superchip), and no reader can infer a per-GPU HBM bandwidth or peak that the part does not have.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph following the three-case host table
quoted_clause: 19 / 21 / 22 — and 32 (KV-only) / 34 (case (ii)) at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy, Ch 16/17 (the ρ = 1 u-only screen reads 30 / 33)

The 33 is only reachable if the N−1 spare is added to the 22-host case but not to the 21-host case (⌈22/0.7⌉ + 1 = 33 versus ⌈21/0.7⌉ = 30), which is an asymmetric application of the same policy. The 32/34 pair at the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy is internally consistent (⌈21/0.665⌉ + 1 = 32; ⌈22/0.665⌉ + 1 = 34), so the 'u-only' pair appears to be a different policy applied without being stated.
root_cause: A third screen variant was introduced without its policy being stated, and the arithmetic was not re-derived after the policy changed.
correction: State the u-only policy explicitly (e.g. 'utilization-only, no availability derate, no N−1 spare') and recompute, or correct the pair to 30 / 32. Verify against Ch 16/17, which own these screens.
acceptance_test: Each host-count pair in the sentence is reproducible from a stated policy (utilization derate, availability derate, N−1) and matches the corresponding table in Ch 16/17.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3 'Decode: bandwidth-bound at low batch' (KV-read caveat); compare Ch 7 §3 and Ch 7 §4
quoted_clause: Including it, the decode intensity is (140·B)/(140 + 24·B) FLOP/byte, which *saturates* at ~5.8 FLOP/byte as B→∞

The same letter carries two meanings in adjacent chapters within the same derivation family, and the expression '(140·B)/(140 + 24·B)' mixes a batch count with byte counts without units.

root_cause: Notation was reused across chapters without a global symbol registry.
correction: Rename the batch variable (e.g. n_batch or b) throughout the decode-intensity derivation, and write the expression with units: '(140 GFLOP × n_batch) / (140 GB + 24 GB × n_batch)'. Add a one-line symbol note where the KV formula is first introduced in Ch 7.
acceptance_test: No symbol denotes both bytes and batch size anywhere in the book; the decode-intensity expression carries units on every term.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph following the three-case host table
quoted_clause: ~$155,816.93/mo ≈ $24.97/1K at 21 hosts; ~$162,760.59/mo ≈ $26.08/1K at 22 — illustrative included-cost on the canonical 6.24M-req/mo basis, Ch 16

page_hint: Ch 6 §3, flash-crowd paragraph
quoted_clause: the jobs that arrive behind ~1–2 same-time prefill requests each pay the full 1.08 s prefill of the job(s) ahead of them, so p95 TTFT drifts to ~2.5 s

Under continuous batching — the mechanism the book elsewhere credits with amortizing prefill across requests (Ch 8 §6) — two concurrent 9.2K prefills are largely batched into one or two large GEMM sequences, so the marginal wait is less than a full 1.08 s per queued job. The example is presented as the canonical flash-crowd behaviour, so a reader may carry the serial-prefill model into capacity reasoning.
evidence: Ch 8 §6: 'larger prefill batches ... improve accelerator utilization by forming larger matrix operations, amortizing weight and execution overhead across requests'. Ch 8 §3: 8 × 2,471 ≈ 19,800 tokens/s per host implies a 9.2K prefill takes ~0.47 s of host-wide prefill capacity at 35% MFU, not 1.08 s, when batched.
root_cause: The queueing illustration was written without the batching model the book uses elsewhere.
correction: Add a clause: 'with continuous batching the queued prefills are largely batched, so the marginal wait is less than a full serial prefill per queued job; the serial figure is the conservative bound.'
acceptance_test: The flash-crowd paragraph states whether the queued prefills are served serially or batched, and the p95 figure is labelled accordingly.

page_hint: Ch 9 §3 Options B and C; Ch 9 §5 bullet 1; Ch 9 §6 (11× / 180× ratios)
quoted_clause: A realistic *effective* throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node) ... Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE] ... keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case (§9.3)
observed: Two related inconsistencies. The chapter's own numbers contradict its own rule. (2) The headline 11× and 180× ratios in §6 compare the NVLink *peak* (450 GB/s directional) against *effective* fabric numbers (40 and 2.5 GB/s), so the ratios overstate the on-node advantage by roughly the peak-to-effective factor.
evidence: Recomputation: 40/50 = 0.80; 2.5/3.125 = 0.80; both exceed the chapter's stated 0.40–0.60 band. Ratio check: 6.125/0.5444 = 11.25× and 98/0.5444 = 180.0×, where the denominator is a peak and the numerators are effective. Under the chapter's own 40–60% band, the two-rail HDR ring would be 245/30 ≈ 8.2 s to 245/20 ≈ 12.3 s and the 25 GbE ring 245/1.875 ≈ 131 s to 245/1.25 ≈ 196 s, i.e. ratios of roughly 15–23× and 240–360×.
root_cause: No single convention is declared for the peak-vs-effective denominator, so the worked example, the Common Mistakes heuristic and the architecture-consequence ratios each use a different one.
correction: Declare the convention once (e.g. 'all fabric comparisons use an effective, contention-inclusive bandwidth; the NVLink figure is a peak and is labelled as such') and then either (a) lower the assumed effective values into the 40–60% band and restate the 98 s / 6.1 s / 11× / 180× figures accordingly, or (b) keep the optimistic values but label them explicitly as an upper bound and add a sensitivity band (e.g. 'at 40–60% effective the Ethernet ring is 131–196 s'). Restate the §6 ratios so that peak and effective are never compared in one quotient.
acceptance_test: Every bandwidth figure used in a time or ratio computation in Ch 9 carries an explicit peak/effective label; the effective values used in §3 fall inside the band stated in §5, or §5's band is revised to match; the §6 ratios are either peak-vs-peak or effective-vs-effective, and the text says which.

page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case; Ch 10 §3 (Tensor Parallelism worked example)

page_hint: Ch 10 §3, Tensor Parallelism subsection (formula and the 160-call example)
quoted_clause: the bandwidth term is $T_\text{tp} \approx n_\text{layers} \times 2(N-1)/N \times M_\text{act}/B_\text{dir}$ ... (The bandwidth term above counts one collective per layer; this budget's two-per-block assumption is why the call count below is 160 rather than 80.)

The example then silently corrects the formula by using 160 calls, and the correction is relegated to a parenthetical. correction: Replace n_layers with n_collectives (or n_layers × c where c is the collectives per block, c ≈ 2 for attention+MLP), define c explicitly, and state the assumption inline: 'T_tp ≈ n_collectives × 2(N−1)/N × M_act/B_dir, with n_collectives = c × n_layers and c ≈ 2 for a standard attention+MLP block'. Then the example's 160 follows directly and the parenthetical can be deleted.
acceptance_test: Substituting the example's own inputs into the printed formula reproduces the printed 70 MiB / 0.163 ms; the symbol n_layers no longer appears in a byte-budget formula without a collectives-per-layer multiplier.

page_hint: Ch 10 §1 item 6; Ch 11 §1 item 4; Ch 11 §4 item 3; Ch 12 §2
quoted_clause: separates the compute-bound prefill stage from the bandwidth-bound decode stage onto different GPU pools ... splitting the compute-bound *prefill* stage from the bandwidth-bound *decode* stage onto separate pools, because they bottleneck on different resources ... a FLOP-bound prefill core and a bandwidth-bound decode core running on one pool tells us when to disaggregate ... compute (prefill throughput — prefill is compute-bound, Ch 11), memory bandwidth (decode throughput — decode is bandwidth-bound)

The book's own numbers show the regime is workload-dependent (a 9.2K-token prefill on the canonical 8-GPU host is compute-heavy, but a short-prompt, large-batch decode step can be compute-heavy too, and a large-batch prefill can become memory-bound on activations). A reader can carry away 'prefill is always compute-bound, decode is always bandwidth-bound' as a law, which is exactly the inference the book elsewhere warns against.

correction: State the regime once with its conditions (e.g. 'at long prompt lengths and modest batch, prefill is compute-bound; at small batch and short prompts, decode is bandwidth-bound; both regimes move with batch size, precision and kernel efficiency — see Ch 6 for the crossover arithmetic') and reference it at each of the four sites. Where a specific canonical number is quoted, keep the number and add the condition that produced it.
acceptance_test: Each of the four sites either carries an explicit regime qualifier or points to a single place where the qualifier is stated; no sentence in Chs 10–12 asserts the compute-bound/bandwidth-bound split without a scope.

page_hint: Ch 11 §3 ('When to Disaggregate' paragraph) and Fig 11.3 caption; reconciled by Ch 12 §3
quoted_clause: prefill is **compute-bound** (~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak), decode is **bandwidth-bound** (the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU; under the canonical 8×H100 host it is sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU)

page_hint: Ch 11 §4 (block headed 'Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability'); Ch 11 §6 (block headed 'The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically')
quoted_clause: ### Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability ... ### The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically

The §4 block (hybrid models, looped-depth models, adaptive depth, depth-aware latency, economic denominator) sits inside 'Measurement' but is a capability-qualification argument, not a measurement protocol. The video block's own content is explicitly about a different workload class ('A text prefill/decode split does not prove that the same split is useful here').

Consider moving the video material to an appendix if the chapter is to stay within its stated scope, keeping only the two-paragraph principle in the body.

page_hint: Ch 11 Table 11-2 and its surrounding text; Ch 11 §6 footnotes oct-ix-openvino-paged-attention and oct-ix-sglang-xpu-graph
quoted_clause: #### Table 11-2 — Serving engines by architectural capability (time-sensitive) ... | supported hardware | NVIDIA / AMD / CPU | NVIDIA / AMD | NVIDIA-only | CPU + consumer GPUs | deployment niche |

page_hint: Ch 11 §3 (Prefix Caching paragraph) vs Ch 12 §3 (Candidate (a)) and Ch 12 §7
quoted_clause: Without caching, every request re-runs the ~1.12 PFLOP prefill for those 8K tokens ... a new request reuses the shared-document KV and prefills only the unique query tail — cutting the dominant prefill FLOPs and TTFT for repeated-context traffic ... Prefix caching from Ch. 11 amortizes the prefill attention over repeated requests with the same prompt prefix, reducing effective prefill FLOPs by ~30% at 10 rps average and ~50% at peak 40 rps
observed: Ch 11 describes the saving as 'the dominant prefill FLOPs' — the 8K shared prefix is 8,000/9,200 = 87% of the canonical prefill FLOPs, so a prefix hit removes ~87% of prefill work. Ch 12 then assumes only 30–50% amortization, with no bridge between the two. The book never states the prefix-hit rate that reconciles them, so the reader cannot tell whether 30–50% is a hit-rate-weighted average (implying h ≈ 34% and h ≈ 57% respectively) or a different mechanism. The number is then used to raise the effective prefill ceiling (19.8K → ~28K tok/s) and to rank prefix caching as 'the highest-leverage optimization'.
evidence: Recomputation: 8,000/9,200 = 0.870; saving = 0.870 × h. For a 30% saving, h = 0.345; for 50%, h = 0.575. Ch 12's derived ceiling 19,800/0.70 = 28,286 ≈ 28K tok/s is arithmetically correct given the 30% assumption, but the assumption's provenance is unstated.
root_cause: Two chapters model the same mechanism at different levels of abstraction (per-hit saving vs traffic-weighted average) without an explicit hit-rate parameter linking them.
correction: Introduce the hit rate explicitly in Ch 11 §3 or Ch 12 §3: 'the shared 8K prefix is ~87% of canonical prefill FLOPs; a traffic-weighted saving of 30% therefore implies a prefix-hit rate of ~35% (and 50% implies ~57%)'. Then state the assumed hit rate as the [ASSUMPTION] and the resulting amortization as the [HYPOTHESIS] it already is.
acceptance_test: The 30–50% amortization figure is accompanied by the prefix-hit rate that produces it from the 87% upper bound; Ch 11 and Ch 12 use the same parameterisation of prefix reuse.

page_hint: Ch 12 Table 12-2 ('Monthly fully loaded cost' row) and Ch 12 §8 mini-case; Ch 13 §3 (fleet sizing)

page_hint: Ch 9 §5, first Common Mistake bullet
quoted_clause: (A two‑rank collective over one path is the exception — it can saturate the link; and by the ring model of §3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor.)
observed: For N = 2 the parenthetical is misleading: each link carries (N−1)/N = 1/2 of the tensor per phase, but the two phases together put the entire tensor on the link — so the link does carry 'the whole transfer', which is exactly what the bullet says never happens. The per-phase figure is stated without the phase qualifier.
evidence: Ring accounting: per-phase per-link traffic = (N−1)/N × M; total across both phases = 2(N−1)/N × M. At N = 2: 0.5M per phase, 1.0M total.
root_cause: A per-phase quantity is quoted where the surrounding sentence is about total link traffic.
correction: Rewrite as: '…and by the ring model of §3 each link carries (N−1)/N of the tensor per phase — 2(N−1)/N in total, which for N = 2 is the whole tensor on the link.'
acceptance_test: The parenthetical states the phase scope of the (N−1)/N figure and does not imply that a two-rank link carries less than the full tensor.

page_hint: Ch 9 §3, Option C
quoted_clause: With protocol overhead and multi-node tree contention, a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s.
observed: Option C computes a ring model but justifies the effective bandwidth with 'multi-node tree contention'. The algorithm named in the justification is not the algorithm used in the computation, in a chapter that elsewhere insists that algorithm, transport and topology be labelled separately.
evidence: The same subsection's formula is T_ring ≈ 2(N−1)/N × M/B_eff, a ring; the justification invokes a tree.
root_cause: Copy-paste of a generic contention phrase from a tree-based discussion into a ring-based one.
correction: Replace 'multi-node tree contention' with 'multi-node contention (ring forwarding and shared-fabric contention)'.
acceptance_test: Every effective-bandwidth justification in Ch 9 §3 names the same collective algorithm used in the accompanying formula.

page_hint: Ch 9 §7, 'Optical interconnects and the next generation' bullet

A reader who has internalised the chapter's own convention will read '1.8 TB/s per GPU' as a directional rate and over-estimate transfer times by 2×.

acceptance_test: Every bandwidth figure in Ch 9 carries a direction qualifier; the NVLink 5 figure is stated on the same convention as the H100 figure.

page_hint: Ch 9 §7, 'Optical interconnects and the next generation' bullet
quoted_clause: optical intra‑rack fabrics (400 Gb/s–800 Gb/s per lane) are entering data centers
observed: 'per lane' is the wrong unit for the quantities named. 400 Gb/s and 800 Gb/s are per-port link rates (400G/800G Ethernet, NDR/XDR); a lane in these fabrics is a fraction of a port (e.g. 100 Gb/s per electrical lane in some designs). The phrase will mislead an architect sizing ports or optics.
evidence: Terminology: the chapter's own Table 9-1 uses 'per port' for the same class of figure.
root_cause: Loose unit vocabulary in a chapter whose value proposition is precise unit discipline.
correction: Change 'per lane' to 'per port'.
acceptance_test: All link-rate figures in Ch 9 use 'per port' or 'per GPU' consistently; no figure uses 'per lane'.

page_hint: Ch 9 §5, fifth Common Mistake bullet
quoted_clause: An NDR 400 Gb/s InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s.

correction: Tag the bullet [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] and state the overhead chain explicitly (line code 64/66 plus FEC), so the reader can see where 380 and 180 come from.
acceptance_test: Every quantitative claim in Ch 9 §5 carries an evidence label; the payload-efficiency figures show their derivation.

page_hint: Ch 9 Table 9-1 and its footnote
quoted_clause: | Chip-to-memory | HBM3 (H100) | 3.35 TB/s | ~ns | — | [1P][FACT] | ... | Rack/cluster | InfiniBand HDR/NDR | 200/400 Gb/s ≈ 25/50 GB/s per port | ~us | high capex | [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] | ... *(Hierarchy: bandwidth drops ~2 orders of magnitude from HBM to the cluster fabric ... page_hint: Ch 10 §2 (Mental Model), resource-triangle paragraph
quoted_clause: When a GPU is *idle* waiting, we reach for DP/CP (more work per GPU).
observed: The parenthetical mischaracterises sequence/context parallelism. CP does not give a GPU more work per token; it partitions the sequence so that a context too large for one GPU can be processed at all, at the cost of per-layer attention exchanges. Grouping CP with DP under 'more work per GPU' gives the reader the wrong reason to choose it, and the chapter's own Table 10-1 row for CP ('long contexts, KV too big') says otherwise.
evidence: Internal: Table 10-1 lists CP as splitting 'the token sequence' and fitting when 'long contexts, KV too big'; §1 item 5 says CP is 'useful for very long contexts where the KV cache or attention activations exceed one GPU'.
root_cause: The triangle's three corners (weights / activations / data) were mapped onto strategies, and CP was assigned to the 'data' corner because it also splits a dimension.
correction: Separate the two: 'When a GPU is idle waiting for work, we reach for DP (more requests per GPU). When a single sequence no longer fits one GPU, we reach for CP (split the sequence, pay per-layer attention exchanges).'
acceptance_test: The resource-triangle paragraph's parentheticals match the 'Fits when' column of Table 10-1 for every strategy it names.

page_hint: Ch 10 §4 item 3; compare Ch 13 §4 item 3
quoted_clause: For DP, time the gradient all-reduce as a fraction of step time — if it exceeds ~20%, it caps scaling.

The book's evidence taxonomy requires the label, and the inconsistency means a reader cannot tell whether Ch 10's threshold is a measured rule or a heuristic.
evidence: Cross-chapter: Ch 13 §4 item 3 labels the identical threshold; Ch 10 §4 item 3 and Ch 10 §8 mini-case ('stays under ~20% of step time') do not.
root_cause: The threshold was introduced in Ch 10 and later restated in Ch 13 with a label; the label was not back-ported.
correction: Add '[ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic]' to the Ch 10 §4 threshold and to the Ch 10 §8 mini-case restatement, matching Ch 13.
acceptance_test: The ~20% threshold carries the same evidence label in every chapter where it appears.

page_hint: Ch 9 §3 Option A; Ch 10 §3 (Data Parallelism paragraph)
quoted_clause: Equivalently, 490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided by 900 GB/s gives the same time. ... for $N=8$ the per-rank traffic is $1.75 \times 280 \approx 490$ GB and the sync time is $T_\text{ring} = 2\frac{N-1}{N}\,\text{bytes} / B_\text{eff}$
observed: The numeral '490 GB' denotes two different quantities in adjacent chapters: in Ch 9 it is the total sent-plus-received traffic (245 sent + 245 received) divided by the bidirectional 900 GB/s; in Ch 10 it is the per-rank *send* volume (1.75 × 280) divided by the directional 450 GB/s. Both are correct in their own context, but a reader moving between chapters will reasonably assume the same object and can mis-scale a time by 2×.
evidence: Ch 9: 245 + 245 = 490 GB total, ÷ 900 GB/s bidirectional = 0.544 s. Ch 10: 1.75 × 280 = 490 GB sent (and 490 GB received), ÷ 450 GB/s directional = 1.089 s.
root_cause: The two chapters use the same ring normalisation but different byte-counting conventions, and the coincidence of the numeral hides the difference.
correction: Name the quantity in words at each site: Ch 9 '490 GB of total (sent + received) traffic'; Ch 10 '490 GB sent per rank (and 490 GB received)'. Consider stating the convention once in Ch 9 §2: 'this chapter counts send volume; total link traffic is twice that.'
acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '490 GB' in the book names whether it is send volume or total traffic; a reader can reproduce both 0.54 s and 1.09 s from the stated convention.

page_hint: Ch 11 §6, 'Baseline (canonical single-host)' bullet
quoted_clause: PagedAttention ensures the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV pack fits
observed: PagedAttention does not reduce the 24.1 GB per request; it removes fragmentation so that the aggregate of many such requests packs densely. As written, the sentence attributes a per-request footprint reduction to a mechanism that does not provide one — the exact confusion the book's own terminology discipline (Ch 9's KV-cache/PagedAttention distinction) exists to prevent.
evidence: Ch 11 §3 states the mechanism correctly: 'allocates KV in fixed blocks shared and evicted like page frames, so the ~24.1 GB per request is packed densely and more concurrent requests fit in the same 640 GB node'.
root_cause: A compressed restatement of the §3 sentence dropped the distinction between per-request size and aggregate packing.
correction: Rewrite as: 'PagedAttention removes the fragmentation tax so that the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV packs densely and more concurrent requests fit in the same 640 GB node'.
acceptance_test: No sentence in Ch 11 attributes a per-request KV footprint reduction to PagedAttention.

page_hint: Ch 11 §3, Prefix Caching paragraph
observed: The symbol K is invoked without definition at the point of use, and the arithmetic that follows ('1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200') does not involve K at all. A reader who has not met K in the FLOP model cannot tell what it scales, and the parenthetical as written does not explain the 1.12 PFLOP figure it sits inside.

quoted_clause: the KV cache is ≈15% of total residency at the canonical 9.2K context (24.1/164.1; rising past 20% beyond ~13.4K) and is often the binding constraint.

page_hint: Ch 12, 'The Architect's Question' section, second paragraph
quoted_clause: This distinguishes our approach from the abstract meta-method presented in Ch. 22, which operates at a level of generality that does not instantiate against concrete substrate constraints.

It also adds cognitive load to the one section that must state the chapter's job crisply.

page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Tool-call latency budget' (printed page not verified — chunk supplied without pagination); propagates to Table 19-1, §7, §8
quoted_clause: On 8×H100 the per-turn agent step averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context; tool backends (search, SQL) add 50–150 ms depending on data volume. So per-turn orchestration overhead *L*agent ≈ 220 ms (median).
