evidence: Under the chapter's own per-turn convention each turn is one model invocation that emits γ=65 reasoning tokens and a tool call. Prefill of a 10,000-token context at the canonical 1.08 s / 9,200 tokens = 1.174 s; decode of 65 tokens at 25 ms/token = 1.625 s; so one per-turn model invocation ≈ 2.80 s. Even under a perfect prefix cache the decode of 65 reasoning tokens alone is 1.63 s — 13x the quoted 120 ms. The chapter's own W model agrees: W(3)-W(2) = 17.704-14.561 = 3.14 s and W(2)-W(1) = 14.561-11.520 = 3.04 s of marginal cost per additional turn, versus the 220 ms quoted. The 220 ms figure therefore cannot be 'the LLM's short decision step'; it can only be non-model orchestration overhead.
root_cause: λ_step was introduced as a 'decision step' cost without being reconciled against the per-turn model invocation cost that W already carries. Two different quantities share the name 'per-turn overhead', and the reader is invited to budget 220 ms/turn for a step that the chapter's own arithmetic prices at ~3 s.
correction: Rename λ_step to 'orchestration overhead excluding model compute' and state in the same sentence that the model's own per-turn cost (prefill of the grown prefix + decode of γ) is carried inside W. If a genuine model-step latency is wanted, derive it (e.g. ~1.17 s prefill + 1.63 s decode under no-reuse) and use it consistently. Add a one-line reconciliation table: per-turn cost = model prefill + model decode + tool round-trip + orchestration.
acceptance_test: Every per-turn latency number in Ch 19 (Table 19-1 rows, §4, §7, §8, mini-case) either (a) explicitly excludes model compute and says so, or (b) equals the marginal per-turn cost implied by W (≈3.0-3.1 s). quoted_clause: Under the fallback-inclusive ledger the unconditional p95 equals the conditional p95 — the fallback occupies only the top 2% — mass entirely above p95 — so it cannot move the 95th percentile (under the zero-turn convention it lands exactly on the boundary, CDF(*T* ≤ 2) = 95.0%, and reads *T* = 2 → 440 ms — which is exactly why the convention must travel with the number)

evidence: Caption (printed p.23): 'Low-batch decode (streaming weights per token) lands at ~1 FLOP/byte — the memory-bound side; long-prefix prefill lands at ~41 FLOP/byte — the compute-bound side.' Prose list item (1) on the same page: 'arithmetic intensity places the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte, well to the right of the ~295 ridge'. Figure: the blue 'prefill' triangle sits at the far right of the x-axis, at or beyond the 10000 tick (AI ~ 1e4), not at 41 and not at 2e3. Independent rederivation for the canonical 70B / 9,200-token prefill: FLOPs = 2 x 70e9 x 9200 = 1.29e15; bytes = 140 GB weights + 2.62 MB/token x 9200 = 24.1 GB KV writes = 1.64e11 B; AI = 1.29e15 / 1.64e11 ~ 7.8e3 FLOP/byte (plus ~17% from attention FLOPs -> ~9e3). None of 41, 2e3, or 1e4 is derivable from the canonical numbers as printed; 41 is also implausible on its face, since prefill AI is approximately the number of tokens processed (AI ~ T for large T), so 'long-prefix prefill' cannot be 41.
root_cause: The figure, its caption, and the summary list were authored from three different (unstated) derivations of the same quantity; no single derivation is shown anywhere on the page, so no gate could catch the divergence.
correction: Pick one canonical prefill AI, show its derivation (tokens, FLOPs, bytes, ratio) in the caption or in an adjacent worked example, and make the caption, the marker position, and the prose list item all state that same value. If the intended value is the derived ~8e3, move the marker to ~8e3 and rewrite the caption as '~8x10^3 FLOP/byte — the compute-bound side'. If a different scenario (e.g. a short prompt) is intended, label it as such and plot a second marker rather than silently changing the number.
acceptance_test: One number appears for canonical prefill AI in the caption, in the marker x-position, and in prose item (1); the value exceeds 295 (so 'compute-bound side' is true of the stated number); and a reader can reproduce it from the canonical inputs printed in Ch. 4 / Table 2-1 without consulting another chapter.

figure: FIGURE 2.2 — Prefill and decode on the roofline ridge
issue: The drawn roofline ridge is geometrically inconsistent with its own '~295' crossover label and with the H100 numbers the book uses elsewhere, and the decode marker is drawn ON the ridge, contradicting the figure's own annotation that markers lie below the roof.
evidence: A roofline's bandwidth-limited segment is a straight line in log-log with slope = HBM bandwidth and NO intercept; it must pass through (AI=1, performance = bandwidth). For H100 SXM (FP16 dense 989 TFLOPS, HBM3 3.35 TB/s) the ridge is performance = 3.35e12 x AI, i.e. it crosses the 989 TFLOPS peak at AI = 295 and passes through (1, 3.35e12). The drawn line instead intercepts the y-axis at ~1e12 at AI = 1 and reaches 1e15 at AI ~ 295; those two constraints cannot be satisfied by one straight line (the drawn line implies a bandwidth of ~1.6 TB/s and a crossover at ~600, or, if the drawn slope is 1 decade/decade, a bandwidth of 1 TB/s and a crossover at 1000). The red 'decode' circle at (1, ~1.2e12) is drawn directly on the black ridge line, while the in-figure annotation states 'markers = regime, not measured MFU (real kernels run below the roof)'. The decode marker should sit clearly BELOW the ridge (roofline at AI=1 is 3.35e12; decode at batch 1 achieves ~3.35e12 only in the idealized bandwidth-bound limit, and real kernels sit below it).
root_cause: The ridge was drawn by eye against the axis limits rather than computed from the peak/bandwidth pair, so the intercept, the crossover label, and the marker placement were never reconciled.
correction: Redraw the ridge from the actual numbers: bandwidth-limited segment through (1, 3.35e12) and (295, 9.89e14), with the compute-bound plateau at 9.89e14 (label it 989 TFLOPS, not 1e15). Place the decode marker at (1, ~1e12) clearly below the ridge, and the prefill marker at its derived AI and at a plausible sub-peak performance (e.g. 3-5e14). If the intent was to show decode sitting exactly on the bandwidth roofline, say so in the caption and remove the 'run below the roof' annotation.
acceptance_test: The drawn ridge satisfies performance = 3.35e12 x AI for AI <= 295 and performance = 9.89e14 for AI >= 295; the '~295' label coincides with the drawn crossover; no marker lies on the ridge line unless the caption explicitly says it is on the roofline; the y-axis plateau is labelled 989 TFLOPS.

issue: The figure depicts each token's K/V being appended on the SAME step the token is sampled, contradicting the figure's own caption and the book's prose. A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.'

At minimum, add a one-step offset between the token column and the append box (e.g. a bracket labelled 'appended on the NEXT step') and change the token sub-labels to 'sampled at step t' / 'appended at step t+1'.
acceptance_test: Tracing only the arrows, a reader concludes that a token's K/V is written on the step in which that token is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled; the figure and the printed p.14 prose agree without needing the caption to arbitrate.

issue: The figure's active-per-token line uses '=' where the intended relation is addition, producing a false equation on the page.

acceptance_test: Change the two '=' between the parameter counts to '+' (or '→') so the line reads '11.4B top-2 + 1.4B shared = 12.8B → 25.6 GB always-on'; confirm 12.8B × 2 bytes = 25.6 GB.

figure: FIGURE 3.4 — KV comparison boxes ('dense 12 GB vs MoE 0.6 GB')
issue: The KV comparison is not reproducible from the shape labels printed beside it. A reader who recomputes from '32L/4096H GQA' gets a 5× ratio, not the 20× that the drawn totals imply, so the figure invites a false inference about how much of the KV saving comes from GQA versus from layer count.
evidence: Drawn: 'dense 12 GB vs MoE 0.6 GB' with '8-bit KV set by shape, not routing: 80L/8192H MHA vs 32L/4096H GQA'. Dense: 2 × 80 × 8192 × 1 B = 1.31 MB/token → 12.05 GB at 9,200 tokens (consistent with the house 8-bit KV figure of ~1.31 MB/token). MoE from the printed shape: 2 × 32 × 4096 × 1 B = 0.262 MB/token → 2.41 GB at 9,200 tokens, i.e. 5× dense, not 0.6 GB. 0.6 GB is reachable only with 8 KV heads × 128 head-dim (2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 1 B = 0.0655 MB/token → 0.60 GB), a fact the figure never states.
acceptance_test: Add the KV-head count and head dimension to the shape label (e.g. '32L/4096H, 8 KV heads × 128') and state the context length both totals assume (9,200 tokens), so that 12 GB / 0.6 GB = 20× is derivable from the printed text; otherwise recompute and redraw the two totals. While editing, confirm the italic sub-label is at or above the 8 pt print floor and that the legend text is not smaller than the 8 pt floor.

figure: FIGURE 6.1 — The metric hierarchy as a diagnostic chain
issue: The two vertical arrows appear to point opposite to the directions stated by the caption and by the figure's own inline key. As rendered, the left arrow labelled 'causation' carries its arrowhead at the TOP (next to 'Workload metrics') and the right arrow labelled 'diagnosis' carries its arrowhead at the BOTTOM (next to 'Serving metrics') — i.e. the drawn directions invert the stated causal chain. This is the chapter's central mental model (workload → resource → serving) and the figure is the only place it is drawn.
evidence: Caption: 'Causation runs downward (workload → resource demand → serving behavior); diagnosis runs upward (serving symptom → resource evidence → workload/context).' Inline key under the boxes: 'causation ↓ (workload → resource → serving) | diagnosis ↑ (serving → resource → workload)'. Rendered arrowheads: left vertical line at the 'causation' label terminates in a head at the top edge of the 'Workload metrics' box; right vertical line at the 'diagnosis' label terminates in a head at the bottom edge of the 'Serving metrics' box. The drawn arrows therefore contradict both the caption and the inline key.
acceptance_test: Inspect the source at print resolution and confirm arrowhead placement: the 'causation' arrow must point DOWN (Workload → Resource → Serving) and the 'diagnosis' arrow must point UP (Serving → Resource → Workload). If the heads are as rendered, swap the arrowheads (or swap the two labels) and re-render. Acceptance: drawn arrow directions, inline key, and caption all agree.

figure: FIGURE 3.2 — Dependency order and cache lifetime, panel B
issue: The caption claims out-of-order acceptance, but the diagram shows strictly in-order, left-to-right acceptance. The distinction between 'full-canvas masked sampler' and 'block-causal sampler' is exactly the point of the figure, and the drawing does not exhibit it.
evidence: Caption: 'a full-canvas masked sampler: accepts positions out of order while recomputing bidirectional states'. Panel B draws: fixed prompt → [? ? ? ?] → [A B C ?] → [A B C D]. Every accepted ID appears in its final left-to-right position, and the dashed recompute region always covers the rightmost unresolved cells. No panel shows an ID accepted at a later position before an earlier one, so 'out of order' is asserted in prose but not depicted.
acceptance_test: Either redraw panel B so at least one accepted ID appears out of position (e.g. [? B ? ?] → [A B C D], with the dashed recompute region covering the whole canvas), or amend the caption to 'accepts selected IDs while recomputing bidirectional states' and add a note that the drawing shows one in-order acceptance order for illustration. Acceptance: the caption's ordering claim is either visible in the drawing or explicitly scoped.

issue: The figure's legend vocabulary refers to a 'solid bracket' element that the drawing does not contain, and the one mark that could play that role appears in only one panel. A reader cannot tell which visual element encodes 'finalized prefix state'.

The drawing contains only per-cell boxes (all solid) plus dashed orange recompute rectangles; no bracket element distinguishes finalized from non-finalized state, and the trailing '-' cell in panel A's last group is drawn identically to the finalized 'A B C' cells. A short underline appears beneath the trailing cell of panel A's third group only, and is explained nowhere. figure: FIGURE 3.1 — panel B, masked discrete diffusion
issue: In the masked-diffusion lane the sequence GROWS from three tokens to four across the corruption step, which implies that masking changes sequence length. For a book whose later chapters reason about per-token KV growth and context-length arithmetic, a figure that shows length changing under corruption is a substantive mis-teaching.
evidence: Panel B: left state shows three cells 'A | cat | sat'; the corrupted state shows four cells 'A | M | sat | M'; the fully masked state shows four cells 'M | M | M | M'. acceptance_test: Make all three states the same length (e.g. 'A | cat | sat | sat' → 'A | M | sat | M' → 'M | M | M | M', or 'A | cat | sat' → 'A | M | sat' → 'M | M | M') and keep the three boxes the same width; re-check that the 'M = MASK' note still explains every cell.

issue: Panel A labels its three states; panel B does not, so the reader must map the three boxes by position alone and infer which is clean, which is corrupted, and which is fully masked.

issue: The 'noise prior' state is drawn as a structured histogram rather than an uninformative one, so the visual contrast between structured data and isotropic noise is absent and the reader can infer that the prior retains the data's structure.

The caption calls the drawing 'Conceptual drawing, not a measurement', which does not license a structurally misleading profile.

issue: This caption is set in italic and appears centred, while every other caption in the batch is roman and justified. A single figure breaking the caption convention reads as a production accident.

figure: FIGURE 3.3 — Wan2.2 A14B: active ≠ resident parameters

figure: FIGURE 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue: The HDR series is labelled with a bandwidth basis that contradicts the figure's own title and the ring model's byte count. The figure title promises 'directional bandwidth' and the ring model divides one-directional per-rank sent bytes (245 GB) by a bandwidth, but the legend entry reads 'Two-way HDR: assumed effective 40 GB/s' and the caption repeats 'an assumed effective two-way HDR path'. 'Two-way' in interconnect usage means bidirectional aggregate. If it is read that way, the denominator is a bidirectional figure applied to a unidirectional byte count and the HDR ring time is understated by 2x (245 GB / 20 GB/s per direction = 12.25 s, not 6.125 s). The book's own definition on printed 157 is different again: 'a realistic effective throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node)'. So the number is right but the label names the wrong quantity, and the caption reinforces the wrong term.
evidence: Figure legend: 'Two-way HDR: assumed effective 40 GB/s'; figure header: 'HDR 6,125 ms'; caption: '40 GB/s for an assumed effective two-way HDR path'. Title: 'Ring traffic and directional bandwidth'. Printed 157: 'A realistic effective throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node — the multi-rail effective throughput referenced in §9.2 and Fig 9.1)'. Printed 157 also states HDR payload is '25 GB/s in both link coding', i.e. 25 GB/s per direction, 50 GB/s bidirectional, so 40 GB/s 'two-way' would be 20 GB/s per direction.
acceptance_test: The legend entry, the figure header, and the caption all state the same basis in words that cannot be read two ways, e.g. 'HDR, 2 rails, per-direction effective 40 GB/s'. A reader who computes 245 GB / 40 GB/s = 6.1 s from the figure alone reproduces the printed 6,125 ms, and a reader who reads the label as bidirectional can no longer derive 12.25 s from it. The figure title's word 'directional' is then true of all three series.

figure: Pull-quote callout (unnumbered), lower third of page
issue: The pull-quote's own numbers contradict the linear law it states. It claims '2·70B · L tokens scales linearly — ~0.28 PFLOP at 1K → ~4.5 PFLOP at 32K'. Under 2·70B·L, L=1,000 gives 1.4e14 FLOP = 0.14 PFLOP, not 0.28; and 0.28 PFLOP scaled linearly to 32K would be 8.96 PFLOP, not 4.5. The 32K value (4.59 PFLOP) and the canonical 9.2K value (1.29 PFLOP) are both correct under 2·70B·L, so the '1K' figure is the sole outlier and is 2x too high. A reader who trusts the callout will mis-estimate prefill cost at short context by a factor of two.
evidence: Pull-quote: 'Prefill FLOP also grows with context: 2·70B · L tokens scales linearly — ~0.28 PFLOP at 1K → ~4.5 PFLOP at 32K for a 70B model ... the canonical 9.2K point the prefill is ~1.29 PFLOP (Table 8-1).' Recomputation: 2 x 70e9 x 1000 = 1.4e14 FLOP = 0.14 PFLOP; 2 x 70e9 x 32768 = 4.59e15 = 4.59 PFLOP; 2 x 70e9 x 9200 = 1.288e15 = 1.29 PFLOP (matches the printed 1.29). Ratio check: 4.5 / 0.28 = 16.1, but 32K / 1K = 32.
acceptance_test: The callout's 1K value equals 2 x 70e9 x 1000 / 1e15 = 0.14 PFLOP, and the printed pair (0.14 PFLOP at 1K, 4.5 PFLOP at 32K) satisfies the stated 32x linear ratio. The 9.2K value remains 1.29 PFLOP and agrees with Table 8-1.

figure: n/a — prose page (no figure on this page); reviewed because it supplies the arithmetic that Figure 15.1 (PDF 248) rests on
issue: The attention-FLOP substitution is arithmetically false by two orders of magnitude, and the error inverts the book's own conclusion about which term dominates prefill. The text states: "the per-layer cost is ~ 4 · L² · d_model, where d_model = 8,192. That is 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 = 2.2 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs — the quadratic attention term that grows dominant at long context." The left-hand side of that substitution evaluates to 4 × 84,640,000 × 8,192 = 2.77 × 10¹² FLOPs per layer, not 2.2 × 10¹⁶. Multiplying by the 80 layers named in the preceding clause ("Across 80 layers that is ...") gives 2.22 × 10¹⁴ FLOPs — i.e. the printed exponent should be 10¹⁴, not 10¹⁶. The printed 2.2 × 10¹⁶ is exactly what one obtains with L = 92,000 rather than 9,200, which suggests a dropped factor of ten in L.
evidence: Recomputed: 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 = 2.773e12 (per layer); × 80 layers = 2.218e14. Cross-check against the book's own dense-matmul estimate on the same page: 2P/token with P = 70e9 gives 1.4e11 FLOP/token; over the canonical 9,200-token prompt that is 1.29e15 FLOP. So at the canonical context, attention (2.2e14, or 1.1e14 if the causal half is taken) is roughly 8–17% of the prefill cost, NOT the dominant term. The printed 2.2e16 would make attention ~17× the dense-matmul term and would be the only thing that makes the clause "grows dominant at long context" true at 9,200 tokens. The error therefore propagates into the reader's mental model of the prefill/decode cost split and into the roofline reasoning that Figure 15.1 illustrates.
acceptance_test: The printed substitution must evaluate to the printed result. Correct to "4 × 9,200² × 8,192 ≈ 2.8 × 10¹² FLOPs per layer; across 80 layers ≈ 2.2 × 10¹⁴ FLOPs", and the sentence must then say that attention is a minority term at the canonical 9,200-token context and becomes dominant only at substantially longer contexts (state the crossover, e.g. the L at which 4·L²·d·80 exceeds 1.4e11·L). Separately, state explicitly whether the 4·L²·d convention is causal or dense: causal attention is 2·L²·d per layer, so the factor of two must be declared and used consistently wherever attention FLOPs are compared with the 2P/token dense term.

issue: The y-axis is labelled "Prefill FLOPs / req (GFLOP)" with the no-cache series drawn flat at 100, but the caption describes the same quantity as "a percent of no-cache prefill work". The axis unit and the caption unit are different quantities, and the absolute reading (100 GFLOP per request of prefill) contradicts the book's own canonical arithmetic by roughly five orders of magnitude.
evidence: The book's canonical prefill cost at 70B and 9,200 prompt tokens is 2P/token × 9,200 = 1.4e11 × 9,200 = 1.29e15 FLOP ≈ 1.3 × 10⁶ GFLOP per request — not 100 GFLOP. The same page's prose (printed 227) uses 10¹⁴–10¹⁶ FLOP magnitudes for prefill. A reader who trusts the axis label will believe prefill costs ~100 GFLOP/request and will mis-scale every roofline or capacity calculation built on it; a reader who trusts the caption will read the axis as a percentage. The figure cannot be both.
acceptance_test: Choose one unit and make axis, caption, and any prose agree. Preferred: relabel the y-axis "Prefill FLOPs per request (% of no-cache)" with the no-cache series at 100, and state the absolute no-cache value in the caption (e.g. 'no-cache prefill ≈ 1.3 × 10¹⁵ FLOP at the canonical 70B/9,200-token prompt'). If the absolute GFLOP axis is retained instead, the plotted values must be rescaled to the canonical absolute figures and the caption must drop the 'percent' wording.

figure: FIGURE 12.1 'Candidate architecture synthesis', stage 4 OUTCOME box
issue: The outcome box asserts "CLEARS CAPACITY GATE (a)·(b)" with no qualification, which contradicts Table 12-2 on the facing page: row (b) P/D-disaggregated is judged "conditional final — ✗ throughput at a single prefill host", i.e. the 2 × 8×H100 baseline does NOT clear the capacity gate until the prefill pool is scaled to ~5 hosts. The figure also omits the decode pool that the same table requires for (b), and it omits the open validation gates for (a) and (b) that the caption itself asserts ("each with its own open validation gate (not a settled verdict)"). Only (c) is drawn as gated, so the visual grammar of the figure says 'a and b are approved, c is not'.
evidence: Table 12-2 (printed 202) row (b): verdict 'conditional final — ✗ throughput at a single prefill host (~19.8K ≪ 92K); prefill pool must itself scale to ~5 hosts ... plus a decode pool'. Figure 12.1 (printed 203) stage 4: 'CLEARS CAPACITY GATE (a)·(b) / each needs ~5 hosts of prefill capacity'. The caption's own hedge ('each with its own open validation gate (not a settled verdict)') is contradicted by the figure's green, unqualified outcome box. A reader who reads only the figure will conclude that the 2-pool baseline is capacity-feasible as drawn.
acceptance_test: The OUTCOME box must carry the condition, e.g. 'CLEARS CAPACITY GATE ONLY AFTER SCALING (a)·(b): (b) needs ~5 prefill hosts + a decode pool', and must show that (a) and (b) still carry an open throughput-validation gate (e.g. a small 'throughput gate open' tag), so that the figure's visual state matches the caption's 'not a settled verdict'. The figure must not imply the 2 × 8×H100 baseline passes as drawn.

issue: The drawn 'with prefix cache' curve is concave-decreasing (roughly 100 → 96 → 92 → 88 → 83 → 76 → 65 at reuse 1, 2, 3, 5.6, 10.6, 30, 100), i.e. the saving per decade of reuse grows with reuse. That is the opposite of the amortization law the caption describes. If a prefix of P tokens is shared by r requests and each request also carries an uncached suffix S, per-request prefill falls from (S + P) to (S + P/r), so the ratio f(r) = (S + P/r)/(S + P) is convex-decreasing: the largest saving occurs between r = 1 and r = 10 and the curve then flattens toward S/(S + P).
evidence: Fitting the drawn curve to f(r) is impossible for any S/P: the drawn curve drops 15 points over r = 1→10 but a further 18 points over r = 10→100, whereas f(r) drops monotonically less per decade. For example, with S = 1.475P (which fits the drawn endpoint of 65 at r = 100), f(10) = 64 — the drawn value at r ≈ 10 is ≈ 83. The figure therefore teaches 'prefix caching's per-request saving accelerates with reuse', which is a false model of the mechanism and would mislead a reader sizing prefill headroom.
acceptance_test: Re-plot panel (a) from the stated model: choose and print a prefix/suffix split (e.g. P = 40% of the prompt), plot f(r) = (S + P/r)/(S + P) on the log-r axis, and label the curve with that formula or its parameters. The curve must be monotone and convex-decreasing, with the r = 1 point equal to the no-cache series. If a synthetic curve is retained for illustration, it must still satisfy the amortization shape.

figure: FIGURE 13.1 'The reference-architecture escalation ladder' — de-escalation arrow
issue: The caption twice assigns the de-escalation arrow the colour green ("de-escalation (green) fires on privacy, data sovereignty, and cost"; "de-escalation (green: data sovereignty, cost) moving a workload between tiers"), but the figure draws the de-escalation arrow as a BLUE dashed arrow. In the same figure, green is used for the tier boxes and for the '▼ constraints → STOP' labels, so the caption's colour key is wrong in both directions. The criterion list also disagrees: the figure's arrow label reads "DE-ESCALATE: latency · sovereignty · cost" while the caption says "privacy, data sovereignty, and cost" — 'latency' and 'privacy' are different triggers and the reader cannot tell which is intended.
evidence: Rendered page: the right-hand vertical arrow is blue with a blue dashed stroke; the four tier boxes and the '▼ constraints → STOP' lines are green. Caption (printed 211) refers to green de-escalation and to privacy as the trigger. Two independent mismatches (colour and trigger) in the same element.

If the intended trigger is latency, the caption must say latency; if privacy, the arrow label must say privacy. The caption's colour key must be checked against the rendered figure for every colour it names.

figure: FIGURE 13.1 — placement of the three red escalation-trigger labels
issue: Each red trigger label is drawn in the vertical gap immediately BELOW its own tier box, adjacent to that box's connector into the red escalation arrow: 'demand > ceiling → forces scale-up' sits below the Cluster/fleet box, 'goodput < demand → forces scale-up' below Multi-host, and 'KV residency > cap → forces scale-up' below Single host. Read that way, the Cluster/fleet tier is told to escalate because 'demand > ceiling', which has no destination — the ladder is already at the top. The caption's semantics are the opposite: "Escalation (red) fires when demand, KV residency, or goodput outcomes exceed a tier", i.e. the trigger fires AT a tier and pushes the workload to the next tier up. Under that reading 'demand > ceiling' belongs to the Multi-host tier, not to Cluster/fleet.
evidence: Rendered geometry: label baselines sit below the corresponding box centres and above the next box's top edge, so the nearest antecedent for each label is the box above it. The caption's wording ('exceed a tier') supports the other reading. The figure is therefore readable in two ways, and one of them is incoherent.
acceptance_test: Place each trigger label immediately below the tier at which it fires and add an explicit upward arrow to the next tier (e.g. 'Single host: KV residency > cap → escalate to Multi-host'), or relabel the labels as arrival reasons ('why we moved here'). A reader must be able to state, for each tier, which trigger fires there and which tier it leads to, without consulting the caption.

evidence: Rendered page: four identical green '▼ constraints → STOP' lines, one under each tier box; the caption's two paragraphs mention only escalation triggers, de-escalation criteria, and the measurable-threshold example. No text in the caption or the figure defines the STOP annotation.

figure: FIGURE 15.1 'FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic', AFTER panel
issue: The AFTER panel draws exactly two arrows between the on-chip box and the HBM box (one up, one down), which reads as 'read K/V once, write once' — i.e. a single global K/V pass. The caption explicitly disclaims that reading: "the tile-level on-chip reuse is per-tile: it is not a guarantee that every K/V element is read exactly once globally across all query blocks (the exact number of K/V re-reads depends on the tile scheduling, sequence length, and SRAM size)". The in-panel note ('KV reused per tile — no single global K/V pass') mitigates but does not resolve the conflict, because the drawn arrow count is the strongest visual signal and it encodes exactly the claim the caption retracts.
evidence: Rendered page: BEFORE panel shows a fan of ~7 red arrows; AFTER panel shows 2 green arrows. The caption's scope note is the only textual guard against reading the 2 arrows as 'one global read'. A reader scanning the figure will take the arrow count as the traffic story.
acceptance_test: Label the AFTER arrows with what they represent (e.g. 'read K/V block per tile' and 'write O only') and add an in-panel note that the number of K/V re-reads equals the number of query tiles, or replace the arrow count with a per-tile loop glyph so the figure cannot be read as a single global pass. The figure must not, by arrow count alone, assert a global single-read.

Row (b) says the prefill pool 'must itself scale to ~5 hosts' (which is the peak requirement, since 92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 is derived from the peak load), while row (c) says '~4 avg / ~15 peak hosts at the single-H100 rate'. issue: The price unit 'K' is never disambiguated anywhere in the figure: legend 'managed $20.80/K' and 'price band $15–25/K'; note 'a $15–25/1K price band'; y-axis 'Cost/month (USD, log)' against x-axis 'Requests/month (log)'. figure: FIGURE 19.3 (Turn 4: three state-management policies) — formula note; and the L_T equation in section 19.5

evidence: Figure 19.3 note: 'append-only total = L4 = T*S + T*Y + O_final @ 2.62 MB/token'. With T=4, S=800, Y=65, O_final=300 this gives 3,760 tokens = 9.9 GB, not the 12,960 tokens / 34.0 GB plotted and labelled. The correct form is L_T = L0 + T*S + T*Y + O_final = 9,200 + 800T + 65T + 300 (T=4 -> 12,960 -> 33.96 GB ~ 34.0 GB). The prose on printed p. 306 prints 'L_T = T*S + T*Y + O_final = 9,200 + 800*T + 65*T = 300', which (i) equates a sum that omits 9,200 with a sum that includes it, and (ii) ends in '= 300' where '+ 300' is required. Figure 19.2's legend already uses the correct symbol for the initial context ('initial context (L0)'), so the book's own notation is available.
acceptance_test: Print the formula in both places as L_T = L0 + T*S + T*Y + O_final = 9,200 + 800T + 65T + 300, and verify by substitution that T=0 -> 9,500 tokens -> 24.9 GB and T=4 -> 12,960 tokens -> 34.0 GB, matching the labels in Figures 19.2 and 19.3 exactly.

issue: The caption's takeaway contradicts the derivation note printed on the facing page and the figure's own crossover annotations. The caption says the quadratic attention term 'overestimates the parameterized-linear term at ~53.4K context tokens under full-square counting and ~106.8K under causal-triangle counting, so at 128K it is large but not yet dominant.' By the book's own arithmetic, at 128K the quadratic term is ~2.4x the linear term (full-square) and ~1.2x the linear term (causal-triangle), i.e. it is already the LARGER of the two terms and is 54-71% of total prefill FLOPs. 'Not yet dominant' is false under both conventions and directly contradicts the note on the same spread.
evidence: Printed 340: 'at 128K it is ~2.4x the linear term (linear + quadratic, i.e. 1.2x), and total prefill FLOPs at 128K are ~3.4x the 2N_L baseline'. Independent check: ratio = (N/N*)^2 with N* = 106.8K (causal) gives (128/106.8)^2 = 1.44; with N* = 53.4K (full-square) gives (128/53.4)^2 = 5.74. Either way the quadratic term exceeds the linear term at 128K, so the caption's conclusion is wrong.
acceptance_test: Rewrite the takeaway so it states the crossover as an equality point ('the quadratic term equals the parameterized-linear term at ~53.4K under full-square counting and ~106.8K under causal-triangle counting, and exceeds it beyond those lengths') and replace 'not yet dominant' with the book's own computed ratios at 128K (2.4x full-square / 1.2x causal-triangle, i.e. the quadratic term is already the larger term). Verify the revised sentence against Note 22.1-1 so the caption and note state the same numbers.

figure: FIGURE 22.1 (prefill FLOP crossover), left-panel magenta annotation
issue: The in-figure annotation 'full-square quad overestimates ~53.4x' attaches the number 53.4 to the word 'overestimates', which is a category error and invites a false inference: the reader will conclude that the full-square convention overstates the true attention cost by a factor of 53.4. 53.4K is a crossover CONTEXT LENGTH, not an overestimate factor. The book's own note states the actual overstatement factor is exactly 2x (halving the attention term for the causal mask doubles the crossing).

Printed 340: 'Causal-triangle: halving the attention-part term (see (iii) - a causal mask) doubles the crossing ... so the ~53.4K figure is a property of the full-square convention, and the causal kernel moves it to ~106.8K.' The overstatement factor is 2x; 53.4K is a length on the x-axis.
acceptance_test: Replace the annotation with a statement that names the quantity and the axis, e.g. 'full-square: quadratic = linear at ~53.4K tokens' (and, if the 2x overstatement is worth keeping, state it separately as 'full-square counts 2x the causal attention work'). A reader who has only seen the figure must not be able to conclude that any quantity is overstated by 53.4x.

issue: The derivation note that the figure caption explicitly points to ('Derivation: Note 22.1-1 below') prints a formula that is arithmetically wrong as written: 'L* = N/(n_layers-d) = 70 x (80 x 8,192) = 106.8K tokens'. The printed expression evaluates to 45,875,200, not 106.8K, and the operator is multiplication where division is required. The correct expression is N* = N_params/(n_layers x d) = 70e9/(80 x 8,192) = 106,811 ~ 106.8K (and 53.4K for the full-square convention, N_params/(2 x n_layers x d)). The two crossover values printed in the figure are correct; the formula that produces them is not.
evidence: Printed 340: 'L* = N/(n_layers-d) = 70 x (80 x 8,192) = 106.8K tokens'. Recomputation: 70 x 80 x 8,192 = 45,875,200 (not 106.8K). Correct: 70e9 / (80 x 8,192) = 70e9 / 655,360 = 106,811.5 = 106.8K; full-square: 70e9 / (2 x 655,360) = 53,405.8 = 53.4K. Both printed crossover values are reproduced exactly by the corrected formula, confirming the intended derivation.
acceptance_test: Print the derivation as N* = N_params/(n_layers x d) = 70e9/(80 x 8,192) = 106.8K tokens (full-square: N_params/(2 x n_layers x d) = 53.4K), with N_params defined as 70e9 and the units of N* stated as tokens. A reader must be able to reproduce 53.4K and 106.8K by substituting the printed symbols, with no implicit 10^9 and no inverted operator.

figure: FIGURE 22.1 (prefill FLOP crossover), both panels' y-axes

The left axis is labelled 'Prefill compute (FLOP/request)' but spans 10^-1 to 10^7, which cannot be absolute FLOP/request for the stated 70B model (2 x 70e9 x N is ~1.4e14 at 1K tokens and ~1.4e18 at 10M tokens). The right axis is labelled 'Decode compute (FLOP/token)' with a flat line at ~2e4, whereas 2N for 70B is 1.4e11 FLOP/token. The caption's caveat that 'the panels use different units and are not directly comparable' addresses per-request vs per-token but not the undisclosed scale factors, so a reader comparing the panels' vertical positions will be misled.
evidence: Printed 361: left y-label 'Prefill compute (FLOP/request)', ticks 10^-1..10^7; right y-label 'Decode compute (FLOP/token)', flat line at ~2x10^4; caption 'the panels use different units and are not directly comparable'.
